events.title: The first World Day of Peace
events.shortBlurb: Pope Paul VI opened the civil year with a new annual appeal that the whole world observe the first of January as a day for peace…
body: On 1 January 1968 the Church kept for the first time the World Day of Peace. Pope Paul VI had proposed the observance in a message from the Vatican dated 8 December 1967, asking that the opening day of every civil year be dedicated to thoughts and resolutions of peace among nations and peoples.

He addressed his appeal not to Catholics alone but to all men of good will, hoping that governments, international organizations, and every friend of peace would take up the day as their own; the Church, he wrote, wished simply to launch the idea, with the intention of service and of example.

Paul VI took care that the day not change the liturgical calendar, which reserves the first of January to the Solemnity of Mary, the Mother of God, so that her feast might shed its light upon the prayer for peace. Every year since, the reigning pope has issued a message for the day on a chosen theme of justice and peace.

sources.text: Message of Pope Paul VI for the First World Day of Peace, 1 January 1968 (vatican.va)

events.title: The fall of Granada
events.shortBlurb: The surrender of Granada to the Catholic Monarchs ended nearly eight centuries of Muslim rule in Spain…
body: On 2 January 1492 the city of Granada, the last Muslim kingdom on Iberian soil, surrendered to Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile. Its Nasrid ruler, Muhammad XII, called Boabdil by the Christian chroniclers, handed over the keys of the Alhambra, and the Catholic Monarchs took possession of the city.

The surrender closed the Reconquista, the long recovery of Spain for Christendom that had stretched across nearly eight centuries since the Muslim conquest of 711. By the capitulations signed the previous November, the conquered were promised their property, their laws, and the free exercise of their religion.

The fall of Granada left Spain a single Catholic realm and freed the energies of its monarchs for the wider world; in the same year they dispatched Christopher Columbus across the Atlantic. The promised toleration did not long endure: within a decade the Muslims of Castile and Granada faced the choice of baptism or exile.

events.title: The excommunication of Martin Luther
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, Pope Leo X formally excommunicated Martin Luther, sealing the breach of the Reformation…
body: On 3 January 1521 Pope Leo X issued the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, which pronounced the formal excommunication of Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor of Scripture at Wittenberg who had refused every summons to retract, and cut him off from the communion of the Church.

The sentence carried out the threat of the bull Exsurge Domine of 15 June 1520, which had condemned forty-one propositions drawn from Luther's writings and given him sixty days to recant. Luther had answered on 10 December 1520 by burning the bull, with volumes of canon law, before the Elster Gate of Wittenberg.

The sentence did not end the movement but hardened it. The following April Luther stood before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms and refused again to retract, and in May the Edict of Worms laid him under the ban of the empire. The definitive rupture of Western Christendom was underway.

events.title: The death of St. Edward the Confessor
events.shortBlurb: The pious king of England died, leaving behind the abbey of Westminster and a disputed throne…
body: Edward the Confessor, a son of King Æthelred the Unready and the Norman Emma, had ruled England since 1042 when he died at Westminster on 5 January 1066. He was buried the next day before the high altar of the abbey church of St Peter that he had rebuilt, consecrated only days before, on 28 December 1065.

He died childless, and the succession was disputed at once: the Witan chose Harold Godwinson, crowned in the new abbey on the day of the king's burial, but before the year was out Harold fell at Hastings and William of Normandy seized the throne.

Revered from his death for a life of prayer, almsgiving, and chastity, Edward was canonized by Pope Alexander III in 1161, and on 13 October 1163 his body was translated to a new shrine in the abbey. He was long honored as a heavenly patron of English kings and of the realm itself.

events.title: The birth of St. Joan of Arc
events.shortBlurb: The Maid of Orléans, who would lift the siege of Orléans and see the king crowned before dying at the stake, was born at Domrémy…
body: By ancient tradition Joan of Arc was born on 6 January, the feast of the Epiphany, in 1412 at Domrémy, a village on the Meuse in Lorraine, the daughter of the peasant farmers Jacques d'Arc and Isabelle Romée. France then lay torn by the Hundred Years' War, and an English king claimed her crown.

From about the age of thirteen Joan heard voices she named as Michael the Archangel and Saints Catherine and Margaret, who charged her to raise the siege of Orléans and to lead the dauphin to his anointing. In 1429 she did both: Orléans was relieved on 8 May, and Charles VII was crowned at Reims on 17 July.

Captured at Compiègne in May 1430, she was tried by an ecclesiastical court at Rouen and burned there on 30 May 1431, aged about nineteen. A new trial ordered by Pope Callixtus III annulled the verdict in 1456; Benedict XV canonized her in 1920, and she is honored as a patroness of France.

events.title: The election of Pope Innocent III
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose Lotario dei Conti di Segni, who as Innocent III would raise the medieval papacy to the height of its power…
body: Born about 1161 at Gavignano in the Roman Campagna, Lotario dei Conti di Segni studied theology at Paris and law at Bologna and was made a cardinal at twenty-nine. On 8 January 1198, the day Celestine III died, the cardinals elected him pope, and he took the name Innocent III.

His eighteen-year pontificate raised the medieval papacy to its height. He styled himself the vicar of Christ, arbitrated between rival claimants to the empire, laid England under an interdict in the quarrel over Stephen Langton, and saw the Fourth Crusade, preached at his call, diverted to the sack of Constantinople in 1204.

He gave a first approval to the followers of Francis of Assisi in 1209 and to those of Dominic in 1215, and in November of that year he opened the Fourth Lateran Council, which defined the faith against the Albigenses and bound every Christian to annual confession. He died at Perugia on 16 July 1216.

events.title: The election of Pope Adrian VI
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals unexpectedly chose a Dutch reformer, the last non-Italian pope until the twentieth century…
body: On 9 January 1522 a conclave deadlocked among its factions unexpectedly elected, in his absence, Adrian Florensz Boeyens, born at Utrecht in 1459, a former professor at Louvain who had been tutor to the young Charles V and was then governing Spain as the emperor's regent.

He took the name Adrian VI and remains the only Dutchman to sit on the throne of Peter. Reaching Rome only in August 1522, an austere stranger to its court, he set about cutting its expenses and, through his legate at the Diet of Nuremberg, confessed that the evils afflicting the Church had spread from the Roman see itself.

His earnest reform met resistance on every side, and his reign lasted scarcely twenty months: he died on 14 September 1523 and was buried in the German church of Santa Maria dell'Anima. After him no non-Italian was elected pope until John Paul II in 1978.

events.title: The Rule of the Templars approved at Troyes
events.shortBlurb: A council at Troyes gave the young order of the Knights Templar its rule, launching the first of the military orders…
body: On 13 January 1129 a council assembled at Troyes in Champagne under the presidency of the papal legate, Cardinal Matthew of Albano, with bishops and abbots among whom was Bernard of Clairvaux. Before it came Hugh de Payens with five companions, seeking recognition for the brotherhood he had founded at Jerusalem about 1119 to protect pilgrims on the roads of the Holy Land.

The council gave the knights a written rule, the so-called Latin Rule, which Bernard helped to shape. It bound men under the monastic vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience yet sent them to bear arms in defense of Christendom, a union of monk and knight the Church had never before sanctioned.

With this approval the Templars became the first of the great military orders, and Bernard praised the new knighthood in his treatise In Praise of the New Knighthood. Gifts and recruits poured in until the order grew vast in wealth and power; in 1312, under pressure from King Philip IV of France, Pope Clement V suppressed it.

events.title: The papacy returns to Rome
events.shortBlurb: Pope Gregory XI re-entered Rome, ending nearly seventy years of the popes' residence at Avignon…
body: On 17 January 1377 Pope Gregory XI entered Rome, ending the residence of the popes at Avignon that had lasted since 1309. He had left that city the previous September, deaf to the pleas of the French court, and sailed from Marseille by way of Genoa for Italy.

The return had long been urged as a matter of conscience. Bridget of Sweden had warned earlier popes from Rome, and Catherine of Siena had journeyed to Avignon in 1376 to press Gregory in person, bidding him manfully fulfill the vow he had secretly made to restore the see to its own city.

The homecoming proved fragile, for Rome had suffered in the popes' absence and their court had grown French. Gregory died on 27 March 1378, and the disputed election of Urban VI that followed opened the Great Western Schism, in which rival popes at Rome and Avignon divided Christendom for nearly forty years.

events.title: The Day of Prayer for the Legal Protection of Unborn Children
events.shortBlurb: After the Roe v. Wade decision of this day, the Church in the United States set January 22 aside for prayer and penance for the unborn…
body: On 22 January 1973 the Supreme Court of the United States handed down its decision in Roe v. Wade, striking down the laws of the states that protected unborn children and establishing abortion on demand across the nation. The Catholic bishops answered with immediate and sustained opposition, reaffirming the Church's constant teaching that human life must be respected from conception.

The General Instruction of the Roman Missal appoints the anniversary, in all the dioceses of the United States, a Day of Prayer for the Legal Protection of Unborn Children: a day of penance for violations to the dignity of the human person committed through acts of abortion, and of prayer for the full restoration of the legal guarantee of the right to life.

The observance is kept with Masses, vigils, and acts of reparation, and a proper Mass formulary for the gift of human life may be celebrated. When 22 January falls on a Sunday, the day of prayer is observed on the following day.

sources.text: United States Conference of Catholic Bishops, Day of Prayer for the Legal Protection of Unborn Children (usccb.org)

events.title: The Synod of Worms and the Investiture Controversy
events.shortBlurb: King Henry IV and the German bishops declared Pope Gregory VII deposed, igniting the great struggle over investiture…
body: At Worms on 24 January 1076 the German king Henry IV, defying Pope Gregory VII's decrees against lay investiture and the excommunication of his counselors, gathered the bishops of his realm and renounced all obedience to the pope, declaring Hildebrand deposed from the see of Peter.

Henry's letter to Rome, addressed to Hildebrand, at present not pope but false monk, bade him descend, descend from the apostolic throne. Gregory answered at the Lenten synod that February: he excommunicated the king, declared him deprived of his throne, and released every Christian from the oath of allegiance sworn to him.

The blow shook the kingdom. The Saxons rose again in revolt, and in October 1076 the German princes assembled at Tribur gave the king a year to free himself of the ban on pain of losing his crown, inviting Gregory to judge the quarrel at Augsburg. To keep his throne Henry crossed the winter Alps to seek absolution.

events.title: Henry IV at Canossa
events.shortBlurb: The excommunicated king Henry IV stood three days as a penitent in the snow before Pope Gregory VII to beg absolution…
body: In January 1077 Henry IV of Germany, excommunicated and seeing his supporters fall away, crossed the Alps by the Mont Cenis pass in one of the severest winters on record, with his wife Bertha and their infant son. Gregory VII, traveling north to judge the quarrel, had taken shelter in the Apennine castle of Canossa, held by his ally Matilda, countess of Tuscany.

There, from 25 to 27 January, the king stood before the castle gate as a penitent, barefoot amid ice and snow, fasting and begging admission. On 28 January, moved by the pleading of Matilda and of Abbot Hugh of Cluny, the king's own godfather, Gregory received Henry and loosed him from the ban.

The scene became the lasting emblem of a king humbled before the spiritual power, yet it settled little: within weeks the German princes raised Rudolf of Swabia as a rival king, and the struggle over investiture dragged on until the Concordat of Worms in 1122.

events.title: The confirmation of the Council of Trent
events.shortBlurb: Pope Pius IV confirmed the decrees of the Council of Trent, sealing the reform that would shape Catholic life for four centuries…
body: On 26 January 1564 Pope Pius IV confirmed the decrees of the Council of Trent with the bull Benedictus Deus, reserving their authoritative interpretation to the Apostolic See. The council, the nineteenth ecumenical council of the Church, had met in twenty-five sessions between 13 December 1545 and 4 December 1563, under Popes Paul III, Julius III, and Pius IV, to answer the Protestant Reformation and reform the Church from within.

Its decrees settled Catholic teaching on Scripture and tradition, original sin, justification, the sacraments, the Mass, and the veneration of saints, while its reform canons commanded bishops to reside in their dioceses and ordered that priests be trained in seminaries. Some 255 fathers subscribed the final decrees, and Pius IV established a congregation of cardinals to guard their execution.

The popes who followed carried the council's work into practice: the Roman Catechism of 1566, the revised Breviary of 1568, and the Roman Missal of 1570 under Pius V. The Tridentine settlement governed Catholic worship and discipline for four hundred years, until the Second Vatican Council.

events.title: The death of Charlemagne
events.shortBlurb: The emperor crowned by the pope on Christmas Day, restorer of a Christian empire in the West, died at Aachen…
body: On 28 January 814 Charlemagne, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, died at Aachen and was buried the same day in the great church he had built there. Born in 747, he had ruled the Franks since 768, and on Christmas Day of 800 Pope Leo III had crowned him emperor in St. Peter's at Rome, reviving the imperial dignity in the West.

His wars made him lord of most of Western Christendom: he ended the Lombard kingdom in 774 and subdued the Saxons in a struggle of thirty years. A patron of letters, he gathered scholars such as Alcuin of York to his court, and the Carolingian revival of learning he fostered preserved the classical and Christian inheritance. His biographer Einhard left a vivid portrait of the man.

His only surviving son, Louis the Pious, succeeded him, but the empire did not long outlast his heirs: in 843 his grandsons divided it by the Treaty of Verdun. Yet the ideal he embodied, a Christian emperor ruling in alliance with the Church, governed the political imagination of Europe for a thousand years.

events.title: The Edict of Milan grants toleration to Christians
events.shortBlurb: The emperors Constantine and Licinius agreed to grant Christians freedom of worship, ending the age of persecution in the Roman Empire…
body: In February 313 the emperors Constantine and Licinius met at Milan, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia, and agreed on a common policy of religious freedom for the empire. Their decision, remembered as the Edict of Milan, survives not as a single decree but as a letter of Licinius to the eastern governors, posted at Nicomedia on 13 June 313 and preserved by the Christian writers Lactantius and Eusebius.

The letter granted to Christians, and indeed to all men, the free power to follow the religion of their choice, and it ordered that the churches, cemeteries, and other property seized in the persecutions be restored to the Christian communities without payment. In this it went beyond the edict of the dying Galerius in 311, which had merely permitted Christians to exist.

The agreement marked the decisive turn from persecution to the peace of the Church. Constantine, victor over his rival Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge the previous October, ruled the whole empire alone by 324, and by the end of the century Christianity had passed from a proscribed sect to the favored faith of the Roman state.

events.title: Otto I is crowned Holy Roman Emperor
events.shortBlurb: In St. Peter’s the Saxon king Otto the Great was crowned emperor by the pope, reviving the Western empire and binding it to the papacy…
body: On 2 February 962, the feast of the Purification, Otto I was crowned emperor by Pope John XII in St. Peter's at Rome, reviving the Western empire that had lapsed with the last Carolingians. Born in 912, Otto had been king of the Germans since 936, and his victory over the Magyars at the Lechfeld in 955 had ended their incursions and won him the name of defender of Christendom.

He had first entered Italy in 951, taking the Lombard crown at Pavia and marrying the widowed Queen Adelaide; a decade later he returned in answer to the pope's appeal against King Berengar II, and the imperial coronation followed. In return Otto confirmed by diploma the lands and rights of the Roman Church.

The event refounded what would later be called the Holy Roman Empire and bound the German crown to the papacy for centuries. The alliance quickly soured: when John XII intrigued against him, Otto had the pope deposed by a Roman synod in 963 and set Leo VIII in his place, opening the long medieval contest between empire and papacy. Otto died at Memleben on 7 May 973.

events.title: The death of Rabanus Maurus
events.shortBlurb: The great teacher-monk of the Carolingian age, archbishop of Mainz, died leaving Germany a legacy of learning and the hymn Veni Creator…
body: On 4 February 856 died Rabanus Maurus at Winkel on the Rhine, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, the foremost teacher of the Carolingian age. Born of noble parents at Mainz about 780, he became a monk of Fulda and studied under Alcuin at Tours, who named him Maurus after the beloved disciple of St. Benedict.

Placed over the abbey school of Fulda in 803 and abbot from 822, he made Fulda the greatest center of learning north of the Alps; his pupils included Walafrid Strabo, Lupus of Ferrières, and Otfrid of Weissenburg. His writings embraced commentaries on nearly the whole of Scripture, a treatise on the formation of clergy, and an encyclopedia in twenty-two books, earning him the title Praeceptor Germaniae, the teacher of Germany.

Resigning his abbey in 842 for prayer and study, he was called in 847 to the see of Mainz, where he won the love of his people by his charity in a time of famine. He is traditionally held the author of the hymn to the Holy Spirit, Veni Creator Spiritus, still sung at Pentecost, ordinations, and the opening of conclaves.

events.title: The death of Pope Pius IX
events.shortBlurb: The longest-reigning pope closed a stormy pontificate that defined the Immaculate Conception and saw the loss of the Papal States…
body: On 7 February 1878 Pope Pius IX died in the Vatican, having reigned nearly thirty-two years, the longest pontificate in history after St. Peter's. Born Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti at Senigallia in 1792 and elected in 1846, he had begun as a reforming pope, granting a constitution to the Papal States, until the revolutions of 1848 drove him into exile at Gaeta and returned him a convinced opponent of liberalism.

His pontificate was rich in definition: in 1854 he proclaimed the dogma of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, in 1864 he issued the Syllabus of Errors, and in 1869 he opened the First Vatican Council, which in 1870 defined the pope's infallibility when teaching on faith and morals.

Against the Church the new Italy prevailed: the Papal States were annexed piecemeal, and on 20 September 1870 Italian troops took Rome itself, leaving the pope, who refused every accommodation, styling himself the prisoner of the Vatican. Long venerated for his personal piety, he was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 2000.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Beatification of Pope Pius IX (vatican.va)

events.title: The first apparition at Lourdes
events.shortBlurb: At a grotto in the Pyrenees the Blessed Virgin first appeared to Bernadette Soubirous, calling for prayer and penance…
body: Bernadette Soubirous was the eldest child of a ruined miller, her family lodging in a disused prison cell called the Cachot, when on 11 February 1858 she went with her sister and a friend to gather firewood along the Gave de Pau. At the hollow of Massabielle she heard a sound like a gust of wind and saw in a niche a lady dressed in white.

Neither her parents nor the parish priest, Abbé Dominique Peyramale, believed her at first, and as the crowds grew the civil power moved against the grotto: the police commissioner Jacomet questioned her repeatedly, and in the summer of 1858 officials fenced off the spring under penalty for trespassers. The quarrel became national, and Emperor Napoleon III himself ordered the barriers removed that October.

The Bishop of Tarbes held aloof from the fray, naming a canonical commission in November 1858 that for three years examined the child, the witnesses, and the reported cures. Only on 18 January 1862 did Bishop Laurence pronounce the apparitions 'supernatural and divine.' The skepticism that had fenced the grotto thus gave way to a judgment all the firmer for its delay.

events.title: The Lateran Treaty and the birth of Vatican City
events.shortBlurb: An agreement between the Holy See and Italy settled the “Roman Question” and created the sovereign State of Vatican City…
body: On 11 February 1929 the Lateran Pacts were signed in the Lateran Palace at Rome, ending the Roman Question that had divided the papacy from Italy since the seizure of Rome in 1870. For Pope Pius XI signed his Secretary of State, Cardinal Pietro Gasparri, and for King Victor Emmanuel III the head of the government, Benito Mussolini, after nearly three years of negotiation.

The pacts comprised a political treaty, a financial convention, and a concordat. The treaty recognized the full sovereignty of the Holy See over the new State of Vatican City, a territory of some forty-four hectares around St. Peter's; the convention compensated the loss of the Papal States with 750 million lire and a further billion in state bonds; the concordat regulated the life of the Church in Italy.

The settlement freed the papacy from the self-imposed imprisonment of nearly sixty years and secured its independence of any earthly power. Ratified on 7 June 1929, the treaty was received into the constitution of the Italian Republic in 1948 and, with the concordat revised in 1984, remains the charter of the smallest sovereign state in the world.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Valentine
events.shortBlurb: A Roman priest put to death for the faith on the Flaminian Way, whose name the fourteenth of February has borne ever since…
body: Ancient tradition holds that on 14 February, about the year 269, a priest named Valentine was martyred at Rome under the Emperor Claudius and buried on the Via Flaminia, where a basilica was later raised over his tomb. The Roman Martyrology still commemorates him on that day as a martyr who died on the Flaminian Way.

Of his life almost nothing is known with certainty. Later legends call him a priest of Rome or a bishop of Terni who restored sight to his judge's blind daughter and was beaten with clubs and beheaded for refusing to sacrifice, but the acts are late and unhistorical. In 1969 the Church removed his feast from the General Roman Calendar, while keeping his name among the martyrs.

The day's association with lovers is no part of his story. It arose in the later Middle Ages from the belief that birds paired in mid-February, a fancy Geoffrey Chaucer wove into his Parliament of Fowls, from which the customs of Valentine's Day descend. What the Church honors is simply a witness who gave his life for Christ.

events.title: The election of Pope Leo XIII
events.shortBlurb: The conclave chose Gioacchino Pecci, who as Leo XIII would open the Church’s engagement with the modern age…
body: On 20 February 1878, thirteen days after the death of Pius IX, the cardinals in conclave elected Cardinal Gioacchino Pecci, bishop of Perugia, on the third ballot, and he took the name Leo XIII. Born at Carpineto Romano in 1810, he had governed Perugia for more than thirty years and was camerlengo when Pius died; many expected his age to promise a short reign.

Instead he reigned for twenty-five years, seeking to meet the modern age without yielding the deposit of faith. In 1879 his encyclical Aeterni Patris restored the study of St. Thomas Aquinas as the Church's philosophical standard, and in 1891 Rerum Novarum, on the condition of the working classes, defended the rights of labor and of property alike, founding modern Catholic social teaching.

A tireless promoter of the Rosary, on which he wrote eleven encyclicals, he opened the Vatican Archives to scholars and was the first pope to be filmed and to have his voice recorded. He died on 20 July 1903, aged ninety-three, the oldest pope the Church has known.

events.title: Boniface VIII proclaims the first Holy Year
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Antiquorum habet the pope opened the first Jubilee, offering a full pardon to pilgrims who came to the tombs of the Apostles…
body: On 22 February 1300 Pope Boniface VIII published the bull Antiquorum habet fida relatio, proclaiming the first Jubilee or Holy Year. Moved by pilgrims who told of great indulgences granted a century before, he offered 'the most full pardon of all their sins' to those who, truly penitent and confessed, visited the basilicas of St. Peter and St. Paul, daily for thirty days by Romans and for fifteen by strangers.

Though the bull did not use the word jubilee and looked to a celebration every hundred years, contemporaries called it the annus jubileus, and the name endured. Vast crowds came, among them the painters Cimabue and Giotto and the chronicler Giovanni Villani; Dante, thought to have been a pilgrim, compares the two-way throng on the bridge of Sant'Angelo in the Inferno.

So great was the devotion that the hundred-year interval could not hold: Clement VI kept a second jubilee in 1350, Urban VI fixed the interval at thirty-three years in honor of Christ's life on earth, and Paul II in 1470 decreed the twenty-five years observed ever since.

events.title: The Great Persecution begins
events.shortBlurb: At Nicomedia the edicts of Diocletian opened the last and fiercest persecution of the early Church…
body: On 23 February 303, the feast of the Terminalia, soldiers of the Emperor Diocletian demolished the great church of Nicomedia, his eastern capital, and burned its Scriptures; the next day the first of his edicts against the Christians was published. It ordered the churches razed, the sacred books surrendered, and Christians stripped of rank, office, and civil rights, the opening of the last and severest persecution of the Roman Church.

Three further edicts followed: the clergy were imprisoned, then offered freedom at the price of sacrifice, and in 304 all the empire's inhabitants were commanded to sacrifice to the gods on pain of death. The storm fell heaviest in the East under Diocletian and his Caesar Galerius, while in Gaul and Britain, where Constantius ruled, only the first edict was enforced.

The persecution slackened after Diocletian's abdication in 305, and the dying Galerius granted toleration by his edict of 311, though Maximinus renewed it in the East until his defeat by Licinius. Peace came at last in 313 with the Edict of Milan, and the memory of its countless martyrs the Church has never forgotten.

sources.text: Eusebius, Church History (Book VIII; public-domain translation)

events.title: St. Francis hears the call to apostolic life
events.shortBlurb: At a little chapel near Assisi the young Francis heard the Gospel of the mission and resolved to live it to the letter…
body: On 24 February 1208, the feast of St. Matthias, Francis of Assisi heard Mass at the Portiuncula, the little chapel of St. Mary of the Angels below Assisi that he had helped to rebuild. Born in 1181 or 1182, the son of a rich cloth merchant, he had already renounced his inheritance and was living as a penitent among the lepers and ruined churches of the valley.

The Gospel told of Christ sending the Twelve to preach the kingdom of God with neither gold nor silver, nor scrip, nor two coats, nor shoes, nor staff. Francis took the words as spoken to himself, crying, 'This is what I wish, this is what I seek, this is what I long to do with all my heart,' and casting off shoes and staff girded his tunic with a cord.

He began to preach penance and peace in the streets of Assisi, and companions soon joined him, first Bernard of Quintavalle and then Peter of Cattani, so that the little brotherhood took shape. The next year Francis led them to Rome, where Pope Innocent III gave spoken approval to their way of life, the beginning of the Order of Friars Minor.

sources.text: Thomas of Celano, First Life of St. Francis (public-domain translation)

events.title: The excommunication of Elizabeth I
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Regnans in Excelsis Pope St. Pius V excommunicated the queen of England and deepened the trial of her Catholic subjects…
body: On 25 February 1570 Pius V published the bull Regnans in Excelsis ('He who reigns on high'). It pronounced 'Elizabeth, the pretended queen of England and the servant of crime' a heretic, excommunicated her, declared her deprived of her pretended right to the throne, and absolved her subjects from every oath of allegiance, threatening with the same sentence any who should obey her laws.

The blow came too late for its design: issued in belated support of the rising of the northern Catholic earls, it arrived after that rebellion had been crushed. In London John Felton boldly posted the bull on the gate of the Bishop of London's palace near St Paul's; he suffered death for it on 8 August 1570 and was later beatified among the martyrs of England.

Far from shaking the queen, the bull left every English Catholic a suspected traitor. Parliament answered it with the Treasons Act of 1571, and the Ridolfi plot of the same year hardened the government further; the penal statutes under which Edmund Campion and hundreds more suffered death followed. In 1580 Gregory XIII, at the plea of the Jesuit missioners, quietly suspended the force of the bull for Catholics in England.

events.title: The Edict of Thessalonica
events.shortBlurb: The emperors declared the Nicene faith the religion of the Roman world, naming as its standard the creed held at Rome and Alexandria…
body: On 27 February 380 Theodosius I, newly baptized at Thessalonica by its bishop Ascholius, issued from that city the decree Cunctos populos in his own name and those of his colleagues Gratian and Valentinian II. It commanded all the peoples under their rule to hold the faith 'which the divine Apostle Peter delivered to the Romans', now professed by Pope Damasus and by Peter, bishop of Alexandria.

That faith the edict defined as belief in the single Godhead of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in equal majesty and holy Trinity. Those who kept it were to be called Catholic Christians; the rest, adjudged 'demented and insane', were branded with the name of heretics, to suffer first the judgment of God and then the punishment of the imperial power.

The decree, preserved in the Theodosian Code, made the Nicene faith the religion of the Roman state after long decades of Arian ascendancy in the East. The next year Theodosius gathered the bishops in the First Council of Constantinople, which reaffirmed and enlarged the creed of Nicaea and sealed the triumph of the orthodox faith in the empire.

events.title: The birth of Michelangelo
events.shortBlurb: The sculptor and painter who would carve the Pietà and paint the Sistine Chapel was born in Tuscany…
body: Michelangelo Buonarroti was born on 6 March 1475 at Caprese, a small town in the upper Arno valley where his father was serving as magistrate; the family soon returned to Florence. At thirteen he was apprenticed to the painter Ghirlandaio, and by 1489 he was studying sculpture in the Medici gardens under Bertoldo, a pupil of Donatello, enjoying the favor of Lorenzo the Magnificent.

Called to Rome in 1496, he carved for St Peter's the Pietà of 1499, and for Florence the colossal David. Julius II summoned him back to Rome in 1505; for that pope he painted, almost unaided and against his will, the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel between 1508 and 1512, and for Paul III the Last Judgment on its altar wall, completed in 1541.

In 1546, after the death of Sangallo, Paul III made him chief architect of the new St Peter's; for seventeen years he directed the work and raised the drum of the great dome, which he did not live to see completed. He died at Rome on 18 February 1564, in his eighty-ninth year, and was buried, as he had wished, among his own people in Santa Croce at Florence.

events.title: The death of St. Thomas Aquinas
events.shortBlurb: The Church's greatest scholastic theologian died at Fossanova on his way to a council, his “Summa” left unfinished…
body: Summoned by Gregory X to the Second Council of Lyons, to open in May 1274, Thomas Aquinas set out on foot that January with his treatise Against the Errors of the Greeks. Falling ill near Terracina, he was lodged at the castle of Maienza and then carried to the Cistercian abbey of Fossanova.

There, having received the last sacraments, he died on 7 March 1274, not yet fifty years old. Months before, on 6 December 1273, an ecstasy at Mass had ended his writing: all he had written, he told his companion Reginald, now seemed to him as straw, and the Summa Theologiae broke off unfinished in its treatise on penance.

Born at Roccasecca about 1225, son of the Count of Aquino, he joined the Dominicans against his family's will and studied under Albert the Great at Cologne and Paris, reshaping Christian thought in a short life by wedding the faith to Aristotle's philosophy.

John XXII canonized him in 1323; his relics were translated to Toulouse on 28 January 1369, the day his feast is now kept; the Dominican Pius V declared him a Doctor of the Church in 1567, and Leo XIII named him patron of Catholic schools.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Gregory the Great
events.shortBlurb: The monk-pope who reformed the liturgy, sent missionaries to England, and called himself “servant of the servants of God” died in Rome…
body: Born at Rome about 540, son of the patrician Gordianus and the sainted Silvia, Gregory was prefect of the city about 573; renouncing the world, he founded six monasteries on his Sicilian estates and made his father's house on the Caelian Hill a seventh, St Andrew's, where he took the cowl.

Drawn from the cloister to serve as deacon and then as papal ambassador at Constantinople, he was chosen pope in 590 when plague carried off Pelagius II, and consecrated on 3 September. He fed Rome's poor from the Church's patrimony, made peace with the Lombards, and reformed the Roman liturgy and the chant that bears his name.

His Pastoral Rule, his Moralia on Job, his Dialogues, and his homilies formed the medieval Church; and in 596 he sent Augustine of Canterbury and his monks to preach the Gospel to the English. He styled himself 'servant of the servants of God', the title the popes bear still.

Worn by gout and labor, he died on 12 March 604 and was buried in the portico of St Peter's, acclaimed a saint at once. A Doctor of the Church, his feast is now kept on 3 September, the day of his consecration.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Pope St. Gregory I (the Great)”

events.title: The canonizations of 1622
events.shortBlurb: On a single day Pope Gregory XV raised Ignatius Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Ávila, Philip Neri, and Isidore to the altars…
body: On 12 March 1622 Gregory XV raised five blesseds to the altars in St Peter's, the first time five saints were proclaimed together: Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Society of Jesus; Francis Xavier, its missionary to India and Japan; Teresa of Ávila, reformer of Carmel; Philip Neri, founder of the Oratory and apostle of Rome; and Isidore, a farm laborer of Madrid dead nearly five hundred years.

The five crowned the Catholic renewal that followed the Council of Trent: the new religious orders, the missions overseas, the mystical reform of prayer, and the holiness of ordinary lay life. Spain, which claimed four of the five, bore most of the cost of the festivities, and Isidore's place among them made the day a triumph for Madrid as much as for Rome.

Roman wit had its say through Pasquino, the talking statue: the pope, it observed, had canonized four Spaniards and a saint, Philip Neri being the only Italian. The jest was long remembered; so was the day itself, which fixed the model of the great shared canonizations held at Rome ever since.

events.title: The election of Pope Francis
events.shortBlurb: The cardinals chose Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Buenos Aires, the first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit…
body: On 28 February 2013 Benedict XVI resigned the papacy, the first pope to do so in nearly six hundred years. The conclave that opened on 12 March needed only five ballots: the next evening, 13 March, white smoke rose over the Sistine Chapel, and Cardinal Jean-Louis Tauran announced the election of Jorge Mario Bergoglio, archbishop of Buenos Aires, as the 266th pope, taking the name Francis after Francis of Assisi.

Born in Buenos Aires on 17 December 1936 to a family of Italian immigrants, he was the first Jesuit to sit in Peter's chair, the first pope from the Americas and the Southern Hemisphere, and the first from outside Europe in more than twelve hundred years, since the Syrian Gregory III, who died in 741.

From the balcony he greeted Rome and the world simply, bowed his head, and asked the silent crowd to pray for him before he gave them his blessing. The simplicity of that first night, joined to his chosen name, set the note of poverty and mercy that would mark his pontificate.

events.title: The First Lateran Council
events.shortBlurb: The first general council held in the West met at Rome to confirm the Concordat of Worms and seal the end of the Investiture Controversy…
body: In March 1123 Callistus II presided in person as some three hundred bishops and more than six hundred abbots of the West assembled at the Lateran, the pope's cathedral in Rome. Convoked the previous December, it was the first general council ever held in the West and is reckoned the ninth ecumenical council of the Church.

Its chief work was the solemn confirmation of the Concordat of Worms, agreed the previous September between the pope and the Emperor Henry V, which had ended the long Investiture Controversy. Both originals of the settlement were read before the fathers and ratified, securing the free election of bishops and abbots and reserving spiritual investiture to the Church alone.

The council also promulgated twenty-two disciplinary canons: it voided the ordinations conferred by the antipope Gregory VIII, forbade marriage to clergy in major orders, protected the families and goods of crusaders, and punished those who molested pilgrims on the road to Rome. So deep was the relief at the peace that chroniclers counted the year 1122 as the beginning of a new era.

events.title: The death of St. Benedict of Nursia
events.shortBlurb: The father of Western monasticism, whose Rule ordered the prayer and work of countless monasteries, died at Monte Cassino…
body: Born about 480 at Nursia, of a noble family and the twin brother of Scholastica, Benedict fled the corruption of the Roman schools, living three years as a hermit in a cave above Subiaco, secretly served by the monk Romanus.

Disciples gathered, and after ruling twelve small monasteries he went up, about 529, to Monte Cassino, overthrew a shrine of Apollo, and founded his abbey. There he wrote his Rule, 'a school of the Lord's service', whose life of prayer, reading, and labor under an abbot won the whole West.

All we surely know of his end comes from the second book of Gregory the Great's Dialogues. Six days before it he ordered his grave opened; then, as fever took him, he was carried into the oratory, received the Body and Blood of Christ, and died standing, upheld between his disciples, his hands lifted to heaven.

It was 21 March, in a year tradition reckons as 547; he was laid beside Scholastica, whose soul he had seen ascend as a dove three days after her death. Father of Western monasticism, he was proclaimed a patron of Europe by Paul VI in 1964, and his feast is kept on 11 July.

events.title: The founding of Cîteaux
events.shortBlurb: St. Robert of Molesme and his companions withdrew to a Burgundian wilderness to keep the Rule of St. Benedict in its purity, founding the Cistercian order…
body: On 21 March 1098, the feast of St Benedict, which that year fell on Palm Sunday, Robert, abbot of Molesme, led twenty-one companions out of his Burgundian abbey to a marsh in the diocese of Châlons, ceded to them by Raynald, viscount of Beaune. Among its rushes — cistels in the local speech — they raised the New Monastery, to keep the Rule of St Benedict to the letter.

Authorized by the papal legate Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, the venture survived its founder: within a year Robert was ordered back to Molesme, and the prior Alberic took his place, clothing the monks in their white habit, instituting lay brothers, and winning the protection of the Holy See in 1100. From Cîteaux, in Latin Cistercium, the new observance took its name.

Under Alberic's successor, the Englishman Stephen Harding, Bernard entered in 1112 with thirty companions, and colonies went out to La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond. Stephen's Charter of Charity bound the houses into one order under a yearly general chapter; at his death in 1134 it counted seventy monasteries, and by 1152 some three hundred and fifty.

events.title: The martyrdom of Archbishop Óscar Romero
events.shortBlurb: The archbishop of San Salvador was shot dead at the altar the day after pleading with soldiers to stop killing their people…
body: Born on 15 August 1917 at Ciudad Barrios and ordained in Rome in 1942, Óscar Romero was named archbishop of San Salvador on 23 February 1977, a safe and bookish choice, it was thought. The murder, three weeks later, of his friend the Jesuit Rutilio Grande changed him: his Sunday homilies, broadcast nationwide, began to name the dead, the tortured, and the disappeared of El Salvador's gathering war.

On 23 March 1980, in his last broadcast homily, he appealed to the soldiers: 'I beg you, I beseech you, I order you, in the name of God: stop the repression.' The next evening, 24 March, a single gunman shot him through the heart as he celebrated Mass in the chapel of the hospital of La Divina Providencia, where he lived.

At his funeral in the cathedral, gunfire into the mourning crowd left some thirty dead. A United Nations truth commission later blamed the death-squad leader Roberto D'Aubuisson for ordering his murder. Beatified in 2015, Romero was canonized by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018 — a bishop martyred at the altar for the faith he preached.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Óscar Romero (vatican.va)

events.title: The birth of St. Catherine of Siena
events.shortBlurb: The Dominican mystic who would counsel popes and help return the papacy to Rome was born, by tradition, on the feast of the Annunciation…
body: Born at Siena on 25 March 1347, the feast of the Annunciation, Catherine was the youngest but one of the many children of the dyer Giacomo di Benincasa and his wife Lapa. At seven she vowed her virginity to Christ; at sixteen she took the habit of the Dominican tertiaries, passing three years in a little room of her father's house in prayer and austerity.

Emerging to nurse the sick and serve the poor, she gathered disciples and dictated letters — nearly four hundred survive — to popes and ordinary souls. At Pisa in 1375 she received the stigmata, which at her prayer remained invisible; in 1376 she went to Gregory XI at Avignon, urging him to reform the Church and return to Rome, which he did on 17 January 1377.

In the Great Schism she labored for Urban VI; she dictated her Dialogue in 1378 and, at his summons, went to Rome, where she wore out her strength for the Church's unity, dying there on 29 April 1380, aged thirty-three. Pius II, a Sienese, canonized her in 1461; Paul VI made her a Doctor of the Church in 1970, and John Paul II a co-patron of Europe in 1999.

events.title: The consecration of the Florence Cathedral
events.shortBlurb: Pope Eugene IV consecrated Santa Maria del Fiore as Brunelleschi's great dome, the largest since antiquity, was completed…
body: On 25 March 1436, the feast of the Annunciation and the first day of the Florentine year, Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore in Florence. The church, begun in 1296 to the design of Arnolfo di Cambio on the site of old Santa Reparata, had waited more than a century for its crowning work.

That work was the vast octagonal dome of Filippo Brunelleschi, raised between 1420 and 1436 after he won the commission in a public competition of 1418. Built of brick in a double shell without wooden centering, it spans some forty-four metres and remains the largest masonry dome ever constructed.

For the consecration the composer Guillaume Dufay wrote the motet 'Nuper rosarum flores', whose structure has often been said to mirror the proportions of the church. The day joined faith, civic pride, and the new art of the Renaissance in a single act of dedication.

events.title: The death of Pope Gregory XI
events.shortBlurb: The pope who ended the Avignon exile and brought the papacy home to Rome died there, on the eve of the Great Western Schism…
body: Pope Gregory XI died at Rome on 27 March 1378, aged about forty-nine, little more than a year after bringing the papacy home from Avignon. Born Pierre Roger de Beaufort about 1329, a nephew of Clement VI made a cardinal at eighteen, he had been elected pope at Avignon on 30 December 1370, the seventh and last of the Avignon popes.

Pressed by the letters of Catherine of Siena and by the entreaties of the Romans, he left Avignon on 13 September 1376 and, sailing from Marseille and up the Tiber from Ostia, made his solemn entry into Rome on 17 January 1377, ending nearly seventy years of exile from the apostolic see.

His death forced the conclave that, under pressure from a Roman mob, elected Urban VI within weeks; before the year was out the French cardinals had repudiated that choice and set up a rival, Clement VII, at Avignon. The return Gregory had achieved thus opened the door to the Great Western Schism.

events.title: The birth of St. Teresa of Ávila
events.shortBlurb: The reformer of Carmel, mystic, and first woman named a Doctor of the Church was born at Ávila in Castile…
body: Teresa of Ávila was born on 28 March 1515 at Ávila in Castile, the daughter of Alonso Sánchez de Cepeda, a prosperous wool merchant, and his second wife, Beatriz de Ahumada. At the age of twenty she entered the Carmelite convent of the Incarnation at Ávila, where nearly twenty years of ordinary observance passed before her deeper conversion to prayer.

Grieved by the laxity she saw around her, she founded at Ávila in 1562 the convent of St. Joseph under the primitive rule in strict poverty, the first house of what became the Discalced Carmelites. With John of the Cross, whose first friars settled at Duruelo in 1568, she extended the reform to men, founding seventeen convents in all.

Her writings — the 'Life', 'The Way of Perfection', 'The Interior Castle', and the 'Book of Foundations' — map the degrees of prayer with unmatched directness. She died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582, was canonized by Gregory XV in 1622, and in 1970 Paul VI declared her the first woman Doctor of the Church.

events.title: St. Bernard preaches the Second Crusade at Vézelay
events.shortBlurb: At the pope's bidding, the abbot of Clairvaux roused France to a new crusade, and the king of France took the cross…
body: On 31 March 1146, at the Easter assembly on the hillside of Vézelay in Burgundy, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, preached the Second Crusade before King Louis VII of France, Queen Eleanor, and a great gathering of nobles. Pope Eugene III, once Bernard's own monk, had charged him with the task after Zengi, atabeg of Mosul, took Edessa on 24 December 1144, destroying the first of the crusader states.

The response overwhelmed the supply of cloth crosses, and Bernard is said to have cut up his own habit to make more; the king and his barons knelt to receive the cross. Bernard then carried the preaching into Germany, where he won King Conrad III at Speyer and silenced the monk Rudolf, whose agitation had stirred massacres of Jews in the Rhineland.

The crusade of 1147 to 1149 ended in failure before Damascus, a humiliation Bernard answered in his apology to the pope, set down in the second book of 'De consideratione', where he laid the disaster upon the sins of the crusaders themselves. Edessa was never recovered.

events.title: The death of Pope St. John Paul II
events.shortBlurb: After twenty-six years on the Chair of Peter, the pilgrim pope died as the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday began…
body: Pope John Paul II died at 9:37 in the evening of 2 April 2005, in his private apartment in the Apostolic Palace, aged eighty-four, as the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday — a feast he himself had established in 2000 — was beginning. Born Karol Wojtyła at Wadowice in Poland in 1920, he had been elected on 16 October 1978, the first Polish pope and the first non-Italian in 455 years.

His reign of twenty-six and a half years was among the longest in the Church's history, exceeded only by those of Peter and Pius IX. It gave the Church the Catechism of 1992, fourteen encyclicals, an unprecedented number of beatifications and canonizations, and more than a hundred journeys abroad, while his moral witness played its part in the peaceful collapse of communism in eastern Europe.

His last years, borne openly with Parkinson's disease, were themselves a teaching on suffering. Some four million mourners came to Rome for his funeral on 8 April, where the cry of 'Santo subito' — sainthood now — rose from the square. He was beatified in 2011 and canonized, together with John XXIII, on 27 April 2014.

sources.text: Vatican biography, St. John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: The election that began the Western Schism
events.shortBlurb: The stormy election of Urban VI led to a rival pope and split Latin Christendom for nearly forty years…
body: On 8 April 1378, in a Rome clamouring for an Italian pope after nearly seventy years of French rule from Avignon, the cardinals in conclave chose Bartolomeo Prignano, Archbishop of Bari, who took the name Urban VI. The election, made under the pressure of a rioting crowd, was accepted at first; but Urban's harsh and imperious temper soon alienated the very men who had chosen him.

Withdrawing to Anagni and then to Fondi, thirteen cardinals declared the election invalid as extorted by fear, and on 20 September 1378 elected Robert of Geneva, who took the name Clement VII and re-established his court at Avignon. France, Scotland, Castile, and Aragon rallied to Clement; England, most of Italy, and the Empire held to Urban.

For thirty-nine years Latin Christendom was divided between two — and after the Council of Pisa in 1409, three — rival obediences, a scandal that set saint against saint, with Catherine of Siena for Urban and Vincent Ferrer for Clement. The Council of Constance ended the division in 1417 with the election of Martin V.

events.title: Trent's decree on Scripture and Tradition
events.shortBlurb: The Council of Trent defined the canon of the Bible and the twin sources of the faith…
body: On 8 April 1546, in its fourth public session, the Council of Trent — opened by Paul III on 13 December 1545 — issued its first dogmatic decree, on the sacred books and the traditions of the Church. Against the reformers' principle of Scripture alone, it taught that the truth and discipline of the Gospel are contained 'in the written books and in the unwritten traditions' received from the apostles.

The same decree fixed the canon of Scripture, the first such definition by a general council, receiving 'entire with all their parts' the books of the Old and New Testaments long read in the Church, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and the two books of Maccabees, the so-called deuterocanonical books the reformers had set aside.

It further declared the old Latin Vulgate, hallowed by centuries of use, to be the authentic edition for public reading and disputation, without prejudice to the original texts. These decisions anchored the Catholic answer to the Reformation and governed Catholic teaching on revelation until the Second Vatican Council.

events.title: The encyclical Pacem in Terris
events.shortBlurb: On Holy Thursday, a dying John XXIII addressed his great letter on peace to all people of good will…
body: On 11 April 1963, Holy Thursday, Pope John XXIII signed 'Pacem in Terris', his eighth and last encyclical, which he called his Easter gift. Written six months after the Cuban Missile Crisis, during which the Holy See had served as a channel between Washington and Moscow, it was the first encyclical addressed not only to the bishops and faithful but to 'all men of good will'.

Drafted with the help of Monsignor Pietro Pavan, the letter argued in four parts that peace on earth can stand only upon the order God laid down: the rights and duties of the human person, the right ordering of public authority, equality and mutual respect among nations, and a world community able to serve the universal common good, with disputes settled by negotiation rather than by recourse to arms.

John died of cancer less than two months later, on 3 June 1963. Read far beyond the Church — the first papal encyclical printed in full in the New York Times, and two years later the subject of a United Nations conference of statesmen and scholars — it remains a cornerstone of modern Catholic social teaching.

sources.text: Vatican archive, Encyclical Pacem in Terris of Pope John XXIII (vatican.va)

events.title: The sack of Constantinople
events.shortBlurb: A crusade meant to recover the Holy Land instead stormed and plundered the greatest Christian city of the East…
body: On 12 April 1204 the army of the Fourth Crusade, led by Boniface of Montferrat and the aged Doge Enrico Dandolo of Venice, stormed Constantinople. The expedition, vowed for the Holy Land, had been diverted first to Zara and then, at the suit of the exiled prince Alexios Angelos, to the Byzantine capital, which the crusaders had already besieged once in 1203.

For three days the victors plundered the greatest city of Christendom, sparing neither palaces nor churches; the altars and imperial tombs of the Church of the Holy Apostles were rifled, and the bronze horses of the Hippodrome were carried off to adorn St. Mark's in Venice. Pope Innocent III, who had forbidden any attack on Christians, denounced the sack in furious letters.

The crusaders set Baldwin of Flanders on the throne as Latin emperor, crowned in Hagia Sophia, and divided the empire among themselves, while Greek successor states held out at Nicaea, Trebizond, and Epirus until Nicaea recovered the city in 1261. The breach between the Greek and Latin Churches was never healed; in 2001 and 2004 John Paul II formally expressed sorrow for the crusade.

events.title: The Edict of Nantes
events.shortBlurb: King Henry IV granted the French Protestants a measure of toleration, ending decades of religious war…
body: On 13 April 1598 King Henry IV of France signed the Edict of Nantes, closing nearly forty years of religious war that had begun with the massacre of Vassy in 1562. Henry, raised a Protestant and king of Navarre, had abjured that faith in 1593 to take the French crown; the edict was his settlement between the two religions of his realm.

In ninety-two public and fifty-six secret articles it granted the Huguenots freedom of conscience, public worship in places where it was already established, though not in Paris or at court, and equal access to offices, schools, and hospitals, while restoring Catholic worship where it had lapsed. By separate warrants the crown also granted them about a hundred fortified towns as places of surety, La Rochelle first among them.

The settlement pleased neither side — Pope Clement VIII said that it crucified him — but it gave France nearly ninety years of uneasy peace. Louis XIV revoked the edict in 1685 by the Edict of Fontainebleau, and as many as four hundred thousand Huguenots fled abroad, carrying their skills to England, Holland, and Prussia.

events.title: The cornerstone of new St. Peter's
events.shortBlurb: Pope Julius II laid the first stone of the basilica that would rise over the tomb of the Apostle…
body: On 18 April 1506 Pope Julius II descended into the foundations beside the old Vatican basilica and laid the first stone of the new St. Peter's. The ancient church, built by the Emperor Constantine over the tomb of the Apostle in the fourth century, had stood for some twelve hundred years and was leaning and in danger of collapse.

The first design, by Donato Bramante, imagined a great central church crowned by a dome; the work would pass through the hands of Raphael and Antonio da Sangallo before Michelangelo, appointed chief architect in 1546, gave the building its definitive form, including the mighty dome completed after his death in 1590.

The vast cost was met in part by the preaching of indulgences, whose abuses in Germany helped provoke Luther's protest of 1517. The finished basilica was consecrated by Urban VIII on 18 November 1626, one hundred and twenty years after the first stone, and remains the centre of Catholic worship and pilgrimage.

events.title: Luther before the Diet of Worms
events.shortBlurb: Summoned to recant, Martin Luther refused to disown his writings before the emperor and the empire…
body: On 18 April 1521 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar already excommunicated by Rome, stood for the second time before the Diet of Worms and the twenty-one-year-old Emperor Charles V. Summoned under a safe conduct won by his prince, Frederick the Wise of Saxony, he had acknowledged the day before that the twenty-five books laid on the table were his, and had asked a day to consider his answer.

Asked again whether he would recant, he refused. Unless convinced by the testimony of Scripture or by clear reason, he declared, his conscience was captive to the Word of God, and he could not and would not recant, 'since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience'. The famous 'Here I stand, I can do no other' is traditional but probably a later addition.

On 25 May the emperor issued the Edict of Worms, branding Luther a notorious heretic and banning his writings. By then Frederick's men had spirited him away in a feigned ambush to the Wartburg, where, hidden under the name of Junker George, he spent ten months translating the New Testament into German.

events.title: The election of Pope Benedict XVI
events.shortBlurb: The conclave chose the theologian Joseph Ratzinger to succeed John Paul II…
body: On 19 April 2005, on the fourth ballot of a two-day conclave, 115 cardinal electors chose Joseph Ratzinger, the 78-year-old German dean of the College of Cardinals, as the 265th bishop of Rome. From the loggia of St. Peter's he greeted the crowd as 'a simple, humble laborer in the vineyard of the Lord.'

Born at Marktl am Inn in Bavaria on 16 April 1927 and ordained priest in 1951, he had been a peritus at the Second Vatican Council, archbishop of Munich and Freising from 1977, and from 1981 prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, the closest theological collaborator of John Paul II.

His pontificate gave the Church the encyclicals Deus Caritas Est, Spe Salvi, and Caritas in Veritate and the motu proprio Summorum Pontificum on the older liturgy. Citing failing strength of body and mind, he laid down the office on 28 February 2013, the first pope to do so since Gregory XII in 1415, and died at the Mater Ecclesiae monastery on 31 December 2022.

events.title: The election of Pope St. Gregory VII
events.shortBlurb: The monk Hildebrand became pope and gave his name to a sweeping reform of the Church…
body: On 22 April 1073, at the funeral of Alexander II, the clergy and people of Rome acclaimed as pope the archdeacon Hildebrand, who took the name Gregory VII. Born at Sovana in Tuscany about the year 1015, he had long been the soul of the reforming party in the Roman Church.

His reform struck at simony and clerical marriage and, above all, at lay investiture, the appointment of bishops by secular powers. When the German king Henry IV defied him, Gregory excommunicated and deposed him in 1076; the next January the king stood barefoot in the snow as a penitent at Canossa to win absolution.

Henry renewed the war, set up an antipope, and took Rome in 1084; rescued and then ruined by his Norman allies, Gregory withdrew to Salerno and died there on 25 May 1085, saying, 'I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.' He was canonized by Benedict XIII in 1728.

events.title: Vatican I's constitution Dei Filius
events.shortBlurb: The First Vatican Council defined the harmony of faith and reason against the errors of the age…
body: On 24 April 1870, at its third public session in St. Peter's, the First Vatican Council solemnly approved the dogmatic constitution Dei Filius, on the Catholic faith. Pius IX had opened the council on 8 December 1869, and some seven hundred bishops of the Latin and Eastern rites took part.

Against the rationalism and fideism of the age, the constitution taught that the one true God, creator and lord of all things, can be known with certainty by the natural light of human reason through the things that are made, and that the Christian faith is not opposed to reason: since one and the same God is the source of both, they can never truly conflict.

On 18 July the council issued its second and last constitution, Pastor Aeternus, defining the primacy and infallibility of the Roman Pontiff; the next day the Franco-Prussian War began, and in September Italian troops seized Rome. Pius IX suspended the council on 20 October 1870, and it was never resumed.

events.title: The canonization of John XXIII and John Paul II
events.shortBlurb: On Divine Mercy Sunday, two twentieth-century popes were declared saints together…
body: On 27 April 2014, Divine Mercy Sunday, Pope Francis canonized John XXIII and John Paul II in a single ceremony in St. Peter's Square, before several hundred thousand pilgrims; the retired Benedict XVI concelebrated, the first canonization at which a reigning and a former pope stood together at the altar.

John XXIII, born Angelo Roncalli at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo in 1881, reigned from 1958 to 1963; he summoned the Second Vatican Council, opening it on 11 October 1962, and published the encyclical Pacem in Terris weeks before his death. For him Francis waived the customary second miracle.

John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła at Wadowice in Poland in 1920, reigned from 1978 until his death on 2 April 2005, one of the longest pontificates in history; he was canonized nine years later, after the healing of a Costa Rican woman, Floribeth Mora, was ascribed to his intercession. He himself had established the feast on which they were canonized.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of Sts. John XXIII and John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: Joan of Arc reaches besieged Orléans
events.shortBlurb: The young peasant maid entered the beleaguered city and turned the tide of the Hundred Years' War…
body: On the evening of 29 April 1429 Joan of Arc, a peasant girl of about seventeen from Domrémy in Lorraine, rode into Orléans with a relieving force; the city had been besieged by the English since October, and its fall would have opened all France south of the Loire. She went, she said, at God's command, guided by the voices of Michael the Archangel, Catherine of Alexandria, and Margaret.

Within days the French carried the English bastions, and on 8 May the besiegers struck their camp and withdrew. The deliverance of Orléans turned the tide of the Hundred Years' War; that July the dauphin was crowned at Reims as Charles VII, Joan standing beside the altar with her banner.

Taken by the Burgundians at Compiègne in May 1430 and sold to the English, she was condemned by an ecclesiastical court at Rouen and burned on 30 May 1431. That judgment was annulled in 1456; Benedict XV canonized her on 16 May 1920, and she is honored as a patroness of France.

events.title: The feast of St. Joseph the Worker is instituted
events.shortBlurb: Pius XII set a Christian feast of labor on the first of May, honoring the carpenter of Nazareth…
body: The first of May had been, since the Second International adopted it in 1889 to honor the dead of the Haymarket riot in Chicago, the great festival of socialist and communist labor. In postwar Italy the day carried heavy political charge, and Catholic workers' associations longed for an observance of their own to set against the summons to class struggle.

On 1 May 1955, addressing Italian Catholic workingmen in Saint Peter's Square, Pius XII announced the new feast of Saint Joseph the Worker for that very day. A decree of the Congregation of Rites followed, setting the carpenter of Nazareth before laborers as their model, in whom human work is ennobled because the Son of God once shared it.

The memorial took the place of the Solemnity of Saint Joseph, patron of the universal Church, which Pius IX had instituted in 1870 and which had wandered through Eastertide on a moveable Wednesday. The change belonged to Pius XII's simplification of the calendar in 1955; the older feast of 19 March remained the principal day of Saint Joseph.

sources.text: Vatican, Address of Pope Pius XII on the Feast of St. Joseph the Worker (vatican.va)

events.title: The Finding of the Holy Cross
events.shortBlurb: By ancient tradition St. Helena discovered the True Cross at Jerusalem, a finding long kept on this day…
body: About the year 326 Helena, mother of the Emperor Constantine, made her pilgrimage to the holy places of Jerusalem, where Constantine was clearing away the pagan temple raised over the tomb of Christ. By the tradition recorded by Rufinus and the historians Socrates and Sozomen, her search near Calvary brought to light the wood of the Lord's cross.

Later legend tells that three crosses came to light, the Lord's being known from the thieves' when a dead man revived at its touch. Over the holy places rose the basilica of the Holy Sepulchre, dedicated in 335, and a portion of the wood Helena brought to Rome, where it is venerated to this day in the church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, once her palace.

The Western Church kept the Finding, or Invention, of the Holy Cross on 3 May, distinct from the Exaltation of the Cross on 14 September, a feast joined also to the relic's recovery from the Persians by the Emperor Heraclius about 629. The May feast was removed from the general Roman calendar in 1960.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “Archæology of the Cross and Crucifix”

events.title: The London Carthusian martyrs
events.shortBlurb: The first blood of the English Reformation was shed at Tyburn when three monastic priors refused the royal supremacy…
body: On 4 May 1535, at Tyburn outside London, the first blood of Henry VIII's Reformation was shed: John Houghton, prior of the London Charterhouse, with two fellow Carthusian priors, Robert Lawrence of Beauvale and Augustine Webster of Axholme, and with them Richard Reynolds, a Bridgettine of Syon Abbey, and John Haile, a secular priest.

Their offence was refusal of the Oath of Supremacy, by which the Act of 1534 made the king supreme head of the Church in England. Tried at Westminster and condemned as traitors, they were hanged in their religious habits, cut down alive, and disemboweled; Houghton suffered first, and one of his quarters was nailed over the gate of his own Charterhouse.

Three more of the London community suffered at Tyburn that June, and nine died in prison in 1537. The martyrs of 4 May were beatified under Leo XIII and numbered among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales canonized by Paul VI on 25 October 1970.

events.title: The Sack of Rome and the stand of the Swiss Guard
events.shortBlurb: A mutinous imperial army stormed Rome, and the Pope's Swiss Guard died almost to a man defending him…
body: On 6 May 1527 the unpaid, mutinous army of the Emperor Charles V, Spanish tercios and German landsknechts, many of them Lutherans, stormed the walls of Rome. Their commander, the Duke of Bourbon, fell dead in the first assault, and some twenty thousand leaderless soldiers gave the city over to a sack that raged for days, followed by months of occupation.

Churches were plundered, relics and tombs desecrated, priests and nuns and citizens slain or held for ransom; thousands perished, and the population of Rome fell to a fraction of what it had been. Christendom took the catastrophe as a judgment of God, and the splendor of High Renaissance Rome never wholly returned.

At the Vatican the Swiss Guard, 189 men under Captain Kaspar Röist, made its stand by the obelisk and the steps of St. Peter's while Clement VII escaped by the covered corridor of the Passetto to Castel Sant'Angelo. Of the guard 147 fell, Röist among them; in memory of that stand the new recruits of the Pontifical Swiss Guard are sworn in each year on 6 May.

events.title: The Second Council of Lyons opens
events.shortBlurb: The fourteenth ecumenical council gathered to seek reunion with the Greeks and reform of the Church…
body: On 7 May 1274 Gregory X opened the Second Council of Lyons, reckoned the fourteenth general council of the Church, in the cathedral of St. John. Some five hundred bishops attended, with envoys of the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos and of the Western princes; James I of Aragon came in person.

The council had three ends: aid for the Holy Land, the reform of the Church, and reunion with the Greeks. On 6 July the emperor's envoys accepted the Latin faith, and union between East and West was solemnly proclaimed; it did not outlive the decade, being repudiated at Constantinople after Michael's death.

To end the long vacancies of the papal see, the constitution Ubi Periculum bound the cardinals to strict enclosure in conclave. Thomas Aquinas had died in March on the road to Lyons; Bonaventure, who guided much of the council's work, died there on 15 July, two days before it closed.

events.title: The apparition of St. Michael at Monte Gargano
events.shortBlurb: By ancient tradition the Archangel Michael appeared on Monte Gargano, giving rise to one of the great western shrines…
body: According to the ancient Liber de Apparitione, about the year 490 a rich man of Siponto, hunting a stray bull, found it kneeling at the mouth of a cave on Monte Gargano in Apulia, and the arrow he loosed at the beast turned back upon the archer. After three days of fasting, Michael the Archangel appeared to Lawrence, bishop of Siponto, and claimed the cave for his own.

The grotto was never dedicated by human hands, the Archangel declaring that he had consecrated it himself; it became the sanctuary of Monte Sant'Angelo, the oldest shrine of the Archangel in the West. The feast of 8 May was joined to the memory of a victory over the pagan besiegers of Siponto, won through his aid.

From Gargano the veneration of Michael spread through the Latin Church, and for fifteen centuries the mountain shrine drew pilgrims of every age, Lombard kings, Norman knights, popes, and crusaders who made it a station on the road to the Holy Land.

events.title: The attempt on the life of Pope John Paul II
events.shortBlurb: A gunman shot the Pope in St. Peter's Square on the anniversary of Fatima, and the Pope credited Our Lady with saving him…
body: On 13 May 1981, as John Paul II rode in an open car through St. Peter's Square at the start of his weekly general audience, the Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Ağca fired four shots at close range, wounding the pope in the abdomen and hand; two bystanders were also hurt. Rushed to the Gemelli hospital, he survived five hours of surgery.

The date was the anniversary of the first apparition of Our Lady at Fatima in 1917, and the pope was certain her hand had spared him: 'one hand fired the shot,' he said, 'and another guided the bullet.' A year later he carried one of the bullets to Fatima, where it was set into the crown of the statue of Our Lady.

On 27 December 1983, in a cell of Rome's Rebibbia prison, the pope visited Ağca and forgave him face to face. Sentenced to life imprisonment, the gunman was pardoned by Italy in 2000 at John Paul's wish and sent home to Turkey.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: Leo XIII promulgates Rerum Novarum
events.shortBlurb: The encyclical on capital and labor laid the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching…
body: On 15 May 1891 Leo XIII, pope since 1878, published the encyclical Rerum Novarum, 'Of New Things,' on the condition of the working classes. It mourned that the industrial age had left laborers 'surrendered, isolated and helpless, to the hardheartedness of employers and the greed of unchecked competition.'

Against the socialists it defended the right of private property as founded in nature; against unbridled capitalism it taught that labor is no mere commodity, that the worker is owed a wage sufficient to support himself and his family, that the state must protect the poor, and that working men may lawfully band together in associations of their own.

Leo, born Vincenzo Pecci in 1810, was eighty-one when the letter appeared. It became the charter of modern Catholic social teaching, and later popes have kept its anniversaries: Pius XI with Quadragesimo Anno in 1931, John XXIII with Mater et Magistra in 1961, and John Paul II with Centesimus Annus in 1991.

events.title: Joan of Arc is canonized
events.shortBlurb: Nearly five centuries after she was burned as a heretic, the Maid of Orléans was raised to the altars…
body: Burned as a heretic in the Old Market square of Rouen on 30 May 1431, at nineteen years of age, after a trial presided over by Bishop Pierre Cauchon, Joan of Arc had been dead nearly five centuries when Pope Benedict XV solemnly canonized her in St. Peter's Basilica on 16 May 1920.

Her condemnation had in fact been reversed long before: at the rehabilitation trial of 1455 and 1456, authorized by Pope Callixtus III at the petition of her family, the judgment of Rouen was annulled as iniquitous, and her innocence solemnly declared before the whole Church.

Beatified by Pope Pius X in 1909 and canonized amid the thanksgiving that followed the First World War, she was declared a patroness of France by Pope Pius XI in 1922 — the girl an ecclesiastical court had condemned as a heretic and relapsed now venerated by the whole Church as a virgin.

sources.text: Vatican, Canonization of St. Joan of Arc (vatican.va)

events.title: The birth of Karol Wojtyła
events.shortBlurb: The future Pope John Paul II was born in the Polish town of Wadowice…
body: On 18 May 1920 Karol Józef Wojtyła was born at Wadowice in southern Poland, the second son of a retired infantry officer. He lost his mother Emilia in 1929, his elder brother Edmund, a physician, to scarlet fever in 1932, and his father in 1941, and was left alone before his twenty-first year.

Under the German occupation he labored in a quarry and then in the Solvay chemical works, studying secretly in the clandestine seminary of Kraków kept by Cardinal Adam Sapieha. He was ordained a priest on 1 November 1946, became Archbishop of Kraków in 1964, and was made a cardinal in 1967.

On 16 October 1978 the conclave elected him pope, the first non-Italian in 455 years, and he took the name John Paul II. His pontificate of nearly twenty-seven years ended with his death on 2 April 2005; he was canonized by Pope Francis on 27 April 2014, together with Pope John XXIII.

sources.text: Vatican biography of Pope St. John Paul II (vatican.va)

events.title: The First Council of Nicaea opens
events.shortBlurb: The first ecumenical council of the Church gathered at Nicaea under the Emperor Constantine to answer the Arian denial of Christ’s divinity, and gave the Church its Creed…
body: The first ecumenical council of the Church opened at Nicaea in Bithynia on 20 May 325, summoned by the Emperor Constantine in the year after he had reunited the empire under his sole rule. By the traditional count of Athanasius 318 bishops attended, many bearing the scars of the late persecutions; Pope Sylvester I sent two priest-legates.

The council met chiefly to answer the Alexandrian priest Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature, not co-eternal with the Father. Against him the fathers confessed the Son to be 'consubstantial with the Father' — homoousios — and the creed they framed, expanded at Constantinople in 381, is still sung at Mass.

Nicaea also established a common reckoning for the date of Easter, legislated for the Meletian schism in Egypt, and issued twenty canons of discipline. Arius was condemned and exiled to Illyricum; the sessions ended in the late summer of 325.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “The First Council of Nicaea”

events.title: Ignatius of Loyola is wounded at Pamplona
events.shortBlurb: A cannonball shattered the leg of a Spanish soldier and set in motion the conversion that gave the Church the Jesuits…
body: On 20 May 1521, in the defense of the citadel of Pamplona against a French army, a cannonball shattered one leg of the Basque captain Íñigo López de Loyola and grievously wounded the other. The garrison soon surrendered; the victors, admiring his courage, set his bones and sent him home to the castle of Loyola.
