The convalescence was long and bitter — the badly set leg was broken and reset — and, finding no romances in the house, he read the Life of Christ by Ludolph of Saxony and the Golden Legend of Jacobus de Voragine. Their pages moved him to exchange the service of an earthly king for the service of God.

From that sickbed came the vigil at Montserrat, the year of prayer at Manresa where the Spiritual Exercises took shape, the vows at Montmartre in 1534 with six companions, and the approval of the Society of Jesus by Pope Paul III in 1540. The Jesuits have ever reckoned their beginning from that wound.

events.title: The death of Constantine the Great
events.shortBlurb: The first Roman emperor to embrace Christianity died at Pentecost, baptized on his deathbed…
body: On 22 May 337, the feast of Pentecost, the Emperor Constantine died at the villa of Achyron near Nicomedia, in the thirty-first year of his reign. He had long deferred baptism and received it only weeks before from Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia; he died clothed in the white robe of the neophyte.

Born about 272 at Naissus and proclaimed Augustus by the army at York in 306, he had defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge in 312 and, with Licinius, issued the Edict of Milan in 313, granting the Church peace after the fiercest of the persecutions. In 325 he summoned and presided over the Council of Nicaea.

In 330 he dedicated Constantinople as a new, Christian capital, and there his body was laid in the Church of the Holy Apostles. The empire he divided among his sons had been turned decisively toward the faith, and the age of the martyrs was over.

events.title: The execution of Girolamo Savonarola
events.shortBlurb: The Dominican preacher who had ruled Florence with calls to repentance was hanged and burned in its great square…
body: On 23 May 1498 the Dominican Girolamo Savonarola was hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria at Florence, together with his friars Domenico da Pescia and Silvestro Maruffi; their ashes were thrown into the Arno. He was forty-five years old.

Born at Ferrara in 1452, he entered the Dominicans at Bologna and in 1491 became prior of San Marco in Florence, where his preaching of repentance and his prophecies of chastisement drew the city. After the expulsion of the Medici in 1494 he stood at the head of the republic, and at the carnival of 1497 his followers burned profane books and finery in the 'bonfire of the vanities.'

His denunciation of corruption in high places reached Pope Alexander VI, who excommunicated him in May 1497; when his party fell, he was arrested, tortured into a confession he later retracted, and condemned by ecclesiastical and civil tribunals alike. Never canonized, he has remained a disputed figure — false prophet to some, herald of reform to others.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Gregory VII in exile
events.shortBlurb: The reforming pope of the Investiture Controversy, who brought the emperor to penance at Canossa, died in exile at Salerno…
body: On 25 May 1085 Pope Gregory VII died at Salerno, an exile from Rome. Born Hildebrand at Sovana in Tuscany about 1015, he had been for a generation the moving spirit of reform before his own election to the papacy in 1073, laboring against simony, clerical incontinence, and the lay investiture of bishops.

His struggle with King Henry IV of Germany over investiture reached its height when Henry, excommunicated and deposed, came as a penitent to Canossa in January 1077 and was absolved. War soon returned: Henry's army took Rome in 1084, the antipope Clement III crowned him emperor, and Gregory was rescued only by the Normans of Robert Guiscard, whose sack of the city turned the Romans against him.

Withdrawing south with his Norman allies, he died at Salerno the following year. His last words are recorded: 'I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.' He was canonized in 1606 by Pope Paul V, and his feast is kept on the day of his death.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 25 May

events.title: The fall of Constantinople
events.shortBlurb: The ancient Christian capital of the East fell to the Ottoman Turks, ending the Byzantine Empire after a thousand years…
body: Constantinople, founded by Constantine in 330, had stood for more than eleven hundred years as the capital of the Christian East. By 1453 the empire had shrunk to the city and its surroundings, defended by the most formidable walls in Europe but garrisoned by only six or seven thousand trained men.

Sultan Mehmed II built the fortress of Rumeli Hisari on the Bosporus, had the Hungarian founder Urban cast great cannon, and on 6 April 1453 opened the siege with sixty to eighty thousand men. When the great chain across the Golden Horn kept out his fleet, he hauled ships overland on greased timbers into the harbor.

Before dawn on 29 May, after a fifty-five-day siege, the last assault breached the land walls; the Genoese commander Giustiniani fell wounded, and the emperor Constantine XI perished in the fighting. After three days of sack Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia, the cathedral of Justinian, and made it a mosque.

The Byzantine Empire was at an end after eleven centuries. Mehmed made the city his capital and styled himself Caesar of Rome; Greek scholars and manuscripts moved westward to feed the Renaissance, while Ottoman power pressed upon Christian Europe for generations.

sources.text: Gibbon, Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (public domain)

events.title: The death of Pope St. John XXIII
events.shortBlurb: The “Good Pope” who summoned the Second Vatican Council died on the Monday after Pentecost, mourned across the world…
body: On the evening of 3 June 1963, the Monday after Pentecost, Pope John XXIII died in the Vatican, aged eighty-one, of cancer of the stomach. Born Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli at Sotto il Monte near Bergamo in 1881, he had been elected in October 1958 at seventy-six and was widely expected to be a caretaker pope.

Instead he announced, in January 1959, an ecumenical council, and on 11 October 1962 he opened the Second Vatican Council, calling the Church to renewal and to the reading of the signs of the times. His last encyclical, Pacem in Terris of April 1963, was addressed not to the hierarchy alone but to all men of good will.

His death — mourned far beyond the bounds of the Catholic world — ended a pontificate of less than five years that had changed the Church's course. 'Good Pope John' was beatified by John Paul II in 2000 and canonized by Pope Francis on 27 April 2014.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. John XXIII (vatican.va)

events.title: The election of Clement V
events.shortBlurb: The choice of a French archbishop who would settle the papacy at Avignon began the Church's long exile from Rome…
body: On 5 June 1305, after an eleven-month conclave at Perugia following the death of Benedict XI, the cardinals chose Bertrand de Got, Archbishop of Bordeaux, who took the name Clement V. Not a cardinal and not present at his own election, he was crowned at Lyon that November and never entered Italy as pope.

In 1309 he fixed his residence at Avignon, on lands of the Angevin counts of Provence, beginning the seventy years during which the popes reigned from France. Closely watched by King Philip IV, he summoned the Council of Vienne in 1311, and there in 1312 he decreed the suppression of the Knights Templar, whose order the king had arrested and accused.

Clement died at Roquemaure in April 1314, within months of the king and of the Templar master he had abandoned to the flames. The Avignon residence he had begun endured until Gregory XI returned the curia to Rome in 1377 — an exile that gravely weakened the Church's freedom and prepared the way for the Western Schism.

events.title: The founding of Vatican City State
events.shortBlurb: The Lateran Treaty came into force, restoring the pope's temporal sovereignty and ending the “Roman Question”…
body: Since the seizure of Rome by Italian troops in 1870, the popes had refused to recognize the new kingdom and kept within the Vatican, 'prisoners,' as they styled themselves, of their own palace. On 11 February 1929 the impasse ended: at the Lateran Palace, Cardinal Pietro Gasparri for Pope Pius XI and Benito Mussolini for King Victor Emmanuel III signed the Lateran Pacts.

The settlement comprised three instruments: a treaty recognizing the Holy See's sovereignty over a new State of Vatican City, a concordat regulating the Church's life in Italy, and a financial convention granting 750 million lire in cash and a billion lire in state bonds for the lost territories.

When the ratifications were exchanged on 7 June 1929, the pacts entered into force and the Roman Question was declared definitively and irrevocably settled. The Vatican City — some forty-four hectares, the smallest state in the world — gave the papacy once more a territorial independence in the service of its spiritual mission.

sources.text: Vatican biography and Lateran Treaty documents (vatican.va)

events.title: The sack of Lindisfarne
events.shortBlurb: Norse raiders fell upon the holy island of Lindisfarne, an outrage that shook Christendom and opened the Viking Age…
body: On 8 June 793 heathen seafarers from across the North Sea fell upon the monastery of Lindisfarne, off the Northumbrian coast. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records that they plundered the church of St. Cuthbert, slew some of the brethren, and carried others away — the first great Viking blow upon England.

The island had been a holy place for a century and a half: founded in 635 by the Irish monk Aidan, sent from Iona at the plea of King Oswald, it had been sanctified by its bishop Cuthbert, who died there in 687, and its scriptorium had produced the Lindisfarne Gospels, a glory of Insular art.

News of the sacrilege stunned the Christian world. Alcuin of York, then at the court of Charlemagne, wrote to the brethren that never before had such a terror appeared in Britain as was now suffered from a pagan race. The raid on Lindisfarne is commonly reckoned the opening of the Viking Age in western Europe.

events.title: The death of St. Columba of Iona
events.shortBlurb: The Irish monk who planted the faith among the Picts from his island monastery of Iona died among his brethren…
body: On 9 June 597 Columba — Colum Cille, 'the dove of the church' — died on Iona, in the monastery he had ruled for thirty-four years. Born about 521 at Gartan in Donegal, of the royal Uí Néill kindred, he had founded churches at Derry and Durrow before leaving Ireland.

In 563, after the battle of Cúl Dreimhne with which tradition links his departure, he crossed to Britain with twelve companions and received the island of Iona for his foundation. From its cloister he preached among the Picts, inaugurated Áedán mac Gabráin as king of the Scots of Dál Riata, and formed missionaries for all northern Britain.

His life was written within a century by his kinsman and successor Adomnán, whose Vita Columbae is the chief monument of the Celtic mission. Dying before the altar at the midnight office, he left a mother-house whose sons — Aidan of Lindisfarne among them — carried the Gospel into England; with Patrick and Brigid he is honored as a patron of Ireland.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), 9 June

events.title: The abolition of the Index of Forbidden Books
events.shortBlurb: After four centuries, the Church's catalogue of prohibited books ceased to carry the force of law…
body: The Index Librorum Prohibitorum, the Church's official list of books forbidden to Catholic readers, had stood since 1559, when Paul IV issued the first Roman Index. Twenty editions followed, the last appearing in 1948, and over four centuries the catalogue condemned at one time or another the works of authors from Erasmus to Sartre.

In the reforming climate after the Second Vatican Council, the motu proprio Integrae Servandae of December 1965 recast the Holy Office as the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith. Asked whether the Index still bound, the congregation on 14 June 1966 issued a notification declaring that it kept its moral force but ceased to have the force of ecclesiastical law, its censures being abolished.

The notification, printed in L'Osservatore Romano the next day, left the judgment of books to well-formed consciences and to the vigilance of pastors. Thus quietly ended, after more than four hundred years, one of the most famous institutions of the Counter-Reformation Church.

sources.text: Notification on the abolition of the Index of Books, 14 June 1966 (vatican.va)

events.title: Leo X condemns the errors of Luther
events.shortBlurb: The bull Exsurge Domine censured forty-one propositions of Martin Luther and gave him sixty days to recant…
body: By 1520 the writings of Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar of Wittenberg, had spread through Germany and won him the protection of princes. After a Roman commission examined his works, Leo X on 15 June 1520 issued the bull Exsurge Domine — 'Arise, O Lord' — condemning forty-one propositions drawn from them as heretical, scandalous, false, or offensive to pious ears.

The bull gave Luther sixty days to recant, and Johann Eck published it in Germany that autumn. Luther answered with defiant pamphlets, and on 10 December 1520, the day the grace period expired, he publicly burned the bull together with volumes of canon law at the Elster Gate of Wittenberg.

Leo X replied on 3 January 1521 with the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem, pronouncing his excommunication. Summoned that spring before the emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms, Luther refused to retract, and the breach that became the Protestant Reformation stood open.

events.title: The election of Pope Pius IX
events.shortBlurb: The longest-reigning of the popes was chosen, whose pontificate would define the Immaculate Conception and call the First Vatican Council…
body: On 16 June 1846, a fortnight after the death of Gregory XVI, the cardinals in conclave chose on the fourth ballot Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti, Bishop of Imola, who took the name Pius IX. Born at Senigallia in 1792, he had been made Archbishop of Spoleto at thirty-five and cardinal in 1840.

Hailed at first as a reformer, he was driven from Rome by the revolution of 1848, and the armies of the Risorgimento stripped him of the Papal States, Rome itself falling in 1870. His reign of nearly thirty-two years, ending with his death in 1878, remains the longest in papal history after St. Peter's.

In it he defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception by the bull Ineffabilis Deus in 1854, issued the Syllabus of Errors in 1864, and convoked the First Vatican Council, which in 1870 defined papal infallibility. He was beatified by John Paul II in 2000.

events.title: The Council of Nicaea proclaims the Creed
events.shortBlurb: The first ecumenical council, gathered against Arianism, confessed the Son to be “consubstantial” with the Father…
body: In 325 the emperor Constantine, newly master of the whole Roman world, summoned the bishops of the Church to Nicaea in Bithynia to end the controversy that troubled the East. Arius, a priest of Alexandria, taught that the Son was a creature, made out of nothing and not co-eternal with the Father.

About three hundred bishops — later tradition fixed their number at 318 — gathered that June, nearly all from the Greek East; Pope Sylvester was represented by two priests, and Hosius of Corduba presided. Against Arius the council confessed the Son to be 'begotten, not made, consubstantial (homoousios) with the Father,' and appended anathemas to its creed.

The creed of Nicaea, expanded at Constantinople in 381, is still professed at Mass. The council's twenty canons ordered the Church's discipline, and its settlement that Easter be kept on one and the same Sunday everywhere remains the basis of the Christian calendar.

sources.text: Butler, Lives of the Saints (1866 ed.), General Church history

events.title: The election of Pope Paul VI
events.shortBlurb: Giovanni Battista Montini was chosen to carry the Second Vatican Council to its conclusion…
body: On 21 June 1963, eighteen days after the death of John XXIII, the cardinals elected on the sixth ballot Giovanni Battista Montini, Archbishop of Milan, who took the name Paul VI. Born at Concesio near Brescia in 1897, he had served some thirty years in the Secretariat of State before going to Milan in 1954.

His coronation on 30 June 1963 was the last in papal history. He brought the Second Vatican Council, interrupted by John's death, through three more sessions to its close on 8 December 1965, and then governed the long labor of putting its decrees into effect, including the reform of the liturgy.

The first pope in modern times to travel outside Italy, he journeyed to the Holy Land in 1964 and addressed the United Nations in 1965. His encyclical Humanae Vitae of 1968 met widespread dissent. He died at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978 and was canonized by Pope Francis in 2018.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Paul VI (vatican.va)

events.title: The Council of Ephesus proclaims Mary Mother of God
events.shortBlurb: The third ecumenical council condemned Nestorius and confessed the Virgin Mary as Theotokos, the God-bearer…
body: Nestorius, made Patriarch of Constantinople in 428, unsettled the Church by preaching that the Virgin Mary should be called Christotokos, 'Mother of Christ,' rather than Theotokos, 'Mother of God.' Cyril of Alexandria answered him, Celestine I condemned his teaching at a Roman synod in 430, and the emperor Theodosius II summoned a general council to Ephesus.

On 22 June 431, before the Eastern bishops and the Roman legates had arrived, Cyril opened the council with some two hundred bishops in the church of St. Mary. Nestorius, thrice summoned, refused to appear; that same day the fathers examined his writings, condemned his doctrine, and deposed him from his see.

John of Antioch, arriving late, held a rival assembly and deposed Cyril in turn, but the emperor at length confirmed the council's sentence, and Nestorius died in exile in Egypt about 451. The faith of Ephesus — one Christ, true God and true man, whose mother is therefore truly Mother of God — remains the ground of Catholic devotion to Our Lady.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. John Fisher
events.shortBlurb: The Bishop of Rochester was beheaded for refusing to acknowledge Henry VIII as head of the Church in England…
body: John Fisher, born at Beverley in Yorkshire in 1469, rose from Michaelhouse, Cambridge, to be chancellor of that university and, in 1504, Bishop of Rochester. A scholar and preacher of European fame, he defended the marriage of Queen Catherine and, alone among the English bishops, refused the oath acknowledging Henry VIII as supreme head of the Church.

Imprisoned in the Tower in April 1534, he was created cardinal by Paul III in May 1535, it is said in hope of protecting him; Henry is reported to have answered that the pope might send Fisher a hat, but he should have no head to set it on. Tried at Westminster on 17 June, he was condemned for treason.

On 22 June 1535 he was beheaded on Tower Hill, declaring that he died for the faith of Christ's holy Catholic Church. His friend Thomas More followed him a fortnight later, and Pius XI canonized the two together in 1935.

events.title: The abjuration of Galileo
events.shortBlurb: Galileo Galilei was made to renounce the Copernican doctrine before the Roman Inquisition…
body: Galileo Galilei, born at Pisa in 1564, had been admonished in 1616 not to hold or teach the Copernican doctrine of the earth's motion. When his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared in 1632, he was summoned to Rome and tried by the Roman Inquisition.

On 22 June 1633, in the convent of Santa Maria sopra Minerva, the aging philosopher knelt and abjured the doctrine as contrary to Scripture. Judged 'vehemently suspected of heresy,' he was sentenced to formal imprisonment, at once commuted — first to the house of the Archbishop of Siena, then to his own villa at Arcetri near Florence, where he died in 1642.

The sentence made Galileo's name a byword for the supposed warfare of faith and science. On 31 October 1992 John Paul II, closing the work of a commission he had appointed, acknowledged the errors of his judges and called the affair a tragic misunderstanding.

events.title: The Council of Pisa elects a third claimant
events.shortBlurb: Seeking to end the Western Schism, the council deposed two rival popes and elected a third, deepening the crisis…
body: Since 1378 the Western Schism had divided Latin Christendom between rival popes at Rome and Avignon. When neither Gregory XII nor Benedict XIII would give way, cardinals of both obediences abandoned them and, meeting at Livorno in 1408, summoned a general council to Pisa.

The council opened in the cathedral on 25 March 1409 with some five hundred fathers — cardinals, bishops, doctors, and ambassadors of the Christian princes. On 5 June it deposed both claimants, and on 26 June elected in their stead Peter Philargos, a Franciscan of Crete and cardinal of Milan, who took the name Alexander V.

The two deposed popes each kept an obedience of kingdoms, so that Christendom now counted three rival lines. Alexander V died at Bologna within the year, and his successor, Baldassare Cossa, ruled as John XXIII; the Pisan line is reckoned among the antipopes. The schism was healed only at Constance, by the election of Martin V in 1417.

events.title: The martyrdom of Sts. Peter and Paul at Rome
events.shortBlurb: Tradition holds that the two great Apostles gave their lives at Rome under Nero, consecrating the city with their blood…
body: The earliest witness is Clement of Rome, who about the year 96 recalled how Peter and Paul had borne their testimony 'among us' and gone to their reward. Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the Romans soon after, joins their names together, and about 170 Bishop Dionysius of Corinth affirmed that both had taught in Italy and suffered martyrdom at the same time.

Their deaths fell in the persecution Nero loosed after the fire of 64. Origen relates that Peter was crucified head downward at his own plea, judging himself unworthy to die as his Lord had died; Paul, a Roman citizen, perished by the sword. About the year 200 the presbyter Gaius could point out their trophies on the Vatican hill and along the Ostian Way.

Over those trophies rose the basilicas of Saint Peter on the Vatican and Saint Paul Outside the Walls. A Roman calendar of 354 attests their joint memory on 29 June as far back as 258, and excavations beneath Saint Peter's in the 1940s uncovered the ancient monument over the grave long held to be Peter's — the rock on which the Roman Church has built.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), “St. Peter, Prince of the Apostles”

events.title: Pius IX convokes the First Vatican Council
events.shortBlurb: By the bull Aeterni Patris the pope summoned the first general council of the Church in three centuries…
body: On 29 June 1868, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, Pius IX published the bull Aeterni Patris, summoning the bishops of the Catholic world to the first ecumenical council since Trent had closed in 1563. The fathers were called to meet the errors of the age and to strengthen the Church's doctrine and discipline.

The council opened in St. Peter's Basilica on 8 December 1869 with some seven hundred fathers, the largest assembly of bishops the Church had seen. In April 1870 it issued the constitution Dei Filius on faith and reason, and on 18 July, in Pastor Aeternus, it defined the primacy of the Roman Pontiff and his infallibility when speaking ex cathedra.

Two months later, on 20 September 1870, Italian troops breached the walls of Rome, and on 20 October Pius IX suspended the council indefinitely. It was never reconvened, and its projected constitution on the Church and her mission was left unfinished.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Oliver Plunkett
events.shortBlurb: The Archbishop of Armagh was hanged at Tyburn on false charges, the last Catholic martyr to die there…
body: Oliver Plunkett, born at Loughcrew in County Meath in 1625, was educated at the Irish College in Rome, ordained in 1654, and appointed Archbishop of Armagh in 1669. Returning to an Ireland ground down by penal laws, he labored, often in hiding and disguise, to reform his clergy and hold the Church together.

In the panic of the fabricated 'Popish Plot' he was arrested in Dublin in December 1679. When no jury in Ireland would convict him, he was carried to London and tried at Westminster Hall in June 1681, where perjured witnesses swore he had plotted a French landing. He was condemned for high treason.

On 1 July 1681 he was hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn, forgiving his enemies and protesting his innocence — the last Catholic martyr to die there. His head is venerated at St. Peter's, Drogheda. Beatified in 1920, he was canonized by Paul VI in 1975, the first new Irish saint in nearly seven hundred years.

events.title: The Battle of Hattin
events.shortBlurb: Saladin destroyed the army of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, opening the way to the Holy City…
body: In the summer of 1187 Saladin, sultan of Egypt and Syria, invaded the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem and laid siege to Tiberias. Against the counsel of Raymond of Tripoli, King Guy of Lusignan led the whole field army of the kingdom — some twelve hundred knights with their footmen — from the springs of Sepphoris on a waterless march to relieve the town.

On 4 July 1187, on the arid plateau by the twin hills called the Horns of Hattin, Saladin's host closed around the thirst-tormented army and destroyed it. King Guy was taken prisoner, the relic of the True Cross that led the host was captured, Raynald of Châtillon was struck down by Saladin's own hand, and some two hundred Templar and Hospitaller captives were put to death.

The kingdom was left defenseless: town after town and castle after castle fell to Saladin, and on 2 October 1187 Jerusalem itself surrendered. The news shook Christendom, and Gregory VIII's bull Audita tremendi summoned the West to what became the Third Crusade.

events.title: Jan Hus burned at Constance
events.shortBlurb: The Bohemian preacher was condemned by the Council of Constance and burned at the stake…
body: Born at Husinec in southern Bohemia about 1369, Jan Hus took his master's degree at the University of Prague, was ordained priest in 1400, and served as rector of the university and preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel, where his Czech sermons drew great crowds.

Formed by the writings of John Wyclif, he attacked the clergy's morals and challenged received teaching on the Church and the papacy; excommunicated in 1410 and again in 1411, he left Prague and wrote his chief work, De ecclesia. Given a safe-conduct by King Sigismund, he went to the Council of Constance in November 1414, only to be imprisoned within weeks and tried for heresy.

Refusing to recant propositions he disowned, he was degraded from the priesthood and handed to the secular arm, and on 6 July 1415 was burned outside the city, his ashes thrown into the Rhine. Jerome of Prague followed him to the stake in 1416. Bohemia answered his death with defiance, and the Hussite Wars that broke out in 1419 ravaged the kingdom for some fifteen years.

events.title: The execution of St. Thomas More
events.shortBlurb: England's former Lord Chancellor died on the scaffold rather than deny the authority of the Church…
body: Born in London in 1478, Thomas More rose from the bar to the House of Commons, made his name across Europe with Utopia in 1516, and in October 1529 succeeded Cardinal Wolsey as Lord Chancellor, the first layman to hold that office. Unable to approve the king's divorce or his claim over the Church, he resigned in May 1532.

When the Act of Succession required an oath repudiating the pope's authority, More refused it at Lambeth on 14 April 1534 and was committed to the Tower. After fifteen months he was tried for treason at Westminster Hall on 1 July 1535 and convicted chiefly on the word of Richard Rich, whom he openly branded a perjurer.

Sentenced to be hanged at Tyburn, he was spared that shame by the king and beheaded on Tower Hill on 6 July 1535, declaring that he died "the King's good servant, but God's first." Beatified by Leo XIII in 1886 and canonized with John Fisher by Pius XI in 1935, he was proclaimed patron of statesmen and politicians by John Paul II in 2000.

events.title: The Martyrs of Gorkum
events.shortBlurb: Nineteen priests and religious were hanged in Holland for their faith in the Eucharist and the papacy…
body: In June 1572, as the Sea Beggars of the Dutch revolt overran the towns of Holland, nineteen Catholic clergy were seized at Gorkum: eleven Franciscans with their guardian Nicholas Pieck, four secular priests including the pastor Leonard van Veghel, two Norbertine canons, an Augustinian canon, and a Dominican, John of Cologne, who had come to minister to the prisoners and was taken with them.

Carried to Brielle, they were interrogated by William de la Marck, lord of Lumey, who demanded that each renounce the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist and the primacy of the pope. All refused, and although a letter arrived from William of Orange ordering that priests be left unmolested, it was disregarded.

On 9 July 1572 the nineteen were hanged in a turf shed, their relics afterward gathered at Brussels. Beatified by Clement X in 1675, they were canonized by Pius IX on 29 June 1867, the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, whose martyrdom eighteen hundred years before was then being celebrated at Rome.

events.title: The July apparition at Fátima
events.shortBlurb: In the third Fátima apparition Our Lady showed the three children a vision and entrusted them a secret…
body: On 13 July 1917 the Blessed Virgin appeared for the third time to the shepherd children Lucia dos Santos and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta Marto at the Cova da Iria near Fatima, Portugal. In Lucia's account the children were shown a momentary vision of hell, a sea of fire in which demons and the souls of sinners suffer.

"You have seen hell where the souls of poor sinners go," Our Lady told them. "To save them, God wishes to establish in the world devotion to my Immaculate Heart." She foretold a worse war under Pius XI if men did not cease offending God, and promised to return and ask the consecration of Russia to her Immaculate Heart and the Communion of reparation on the first Saturdays.

These words, with a further vision, form the secret of Fatima in three parts, which Lucia committed to writing only in 1941 and 1944; the third part was published by the Holy See in 2000. The apparitions continued on the thirteenth of each month until October, when the promised sign was witnessed by a vast crowd.

sources.text: Vatican account, The Message of Fátima (vatican.va)

events.title: St. Camillus de Lellis dies in Rome
events.shortBlurb: The soldier and gambler turned servant of the sick, founder of the Ministers of the Infirm, died at Rome…
body: Born at Bucchianico in the Abruzzi in 1550, Camillus de Lellis followed his father into soldiering, fought the Turks in the Venetian army, and lost his substance to gambling. A festering leg wound brought him to the hospital of San Giacomo in Rome, and a conversion of heart in 1575 turned the discharged soldier to a life of penance.

Rejected by the Capuchins because of his wound, he devoted himself to the sick of San Giacomo, took Philip Neri as his confessor, and was ordained in 1584. His brotherhood of Clerks Regular, Ministers of the Infirm, recognized by Sixtus V in 1586 and raised to an order by Gregory XIV in 1591, wore a great red cross and vowed to serve the sick even at peril of life.

Camillus died at Rome on 14 July 1614 and was buried in his order's church of Santa Maria Maddalena. Benedict XIV beatified him in 1742 and canonized him in 1746; Leo XIII in 1886 named him, with John of God, patron of the sick and of hospitals, and Pius XI in 1930 extended the patronage to nurses.

events.title: The storming of the Bastille
events.shortBlurb: The fall of the Paris fortress opened the French Revolution and a long ordeal for the Church…
body: On 14 July 1789, after the dismissal of the minister Necker had thrown Paris into turmoil, a crowd of some hundreds of artisans, joined by mutinous French Guards, attacked the Bastille, the royal fortress and state prison in the east of the city, seeking the gunpowder stored within. After four hours of fighting the governor, Bernard-Rene de Launay, capitulated; the prison held only seven prisoners.

De Launay was butchered on his way to the Hotel de Ville, and his head, with that of the prevot Jacques de Flesselles, was paraded on a pike. The fall of the fortress, long the emblem of royal despotism, was hailed across Europe as the opening act of the French Revolution, and the building itself was demolished within months.

For the Church the Revolution brought swift calamity: the confiscation of ecclesiastical property in November 1789, the suppression of the religious orders in February 1790, and the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in July 1790, which divided the French Church against itself. Within four years came the September Massacres of 1792, in which some two hundred priests perished, and the Terror's attempt to abolish Christian worship itself.

events.title: Keble’s “National Apostasy” sermon begins the Oxford Movement
events.shortBlurb: John Keble's Assize Sermon at Oxford against the suppression of Irish bishoprics kindled the movement that led many to Rome…
body: On 14 July 1833 John Keble, fellow of Oriel College and author of The Christian Year, mounted the pulpit of St Mary's, the university church at Oxford, and preached the Assize Sermon under the title National Apostasy. His provocation was the suppression of ten bishoprics of the Church of Ireland by the Whig parliament, which he denounced as the State's usurpation over the divine constitution of the Church.

John Henry Newman, then vicar of St Mary's, ever afterward kept that day as the beginning of the movement of 1833. In September he began the Tracts for the Times, which gave the movement its familiar name of Tractarianism; Edward Bouverie Pusey joined in 1834, lending the weight of his learning and station.

The movement set out to recover the Catholic heritage of the English Church, its sacraments, apostolic succession, and the Fathers, against liberalism and popular Protestantism alike. Its logic carried many beyond the Establishment: condemned for his Tract 90 in 1841, Newman withdrew to Littlemore and was received into the Catholic Church on 9 October 1845, and many others followed where he had led.

events.title: The First Crusade captures Jerusalem
events.shortBlurb: After a five-week siege the armies of the First Crusade took the Holy City, the goal proclaimed at Clermont four years before…
body: Summoned by Pope Urban II at Clermont in November 1095, the armies of the First Crusade reached Jerusalem in June 1099, reduced by three years of marching and battle to perhaps thirteen thousand fighting men. The city, held by the Fatimids of Egypt, was invested on 7 June amid summer heat and thirst.

On 15 July 1099, after five weeks of siege, the crusaders breached the northern wall near the siege tower of Godfrey of Bouillon and poured into the city. The sack that followed was merciless: Muslims and Jews alike were massacred in numbers the chroniclers reckoned in the tens of thousands, a butchery the victors themselves recorded without shame.

A week later Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen ruler of the conquered city, refusing the name of king and taking instead the title Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre. Thus was founded the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, which endured until Saladin's victory at Hattin in 1187, while the last crusader foothold in the East, Acre, survived until 1291.

events.title: The death of St. Bonaventure at Lyons
events.shortBlurb: The Seraphic Doctor died during the Second Council of Lyons he had helped to guide…
body: Gregory X had called the fourteenth general council to Lyons to succor the Holy Land, reform Christian life, and end the Greek schism; it opened on 7 May 1274 with the pope himself presiding. Thomas Aquinas died on the road to the council, at Fossanova that March, and it fell to Bonaventure, Cardinal-Bishop of Albano, to prepare the agenda and conduct the conferences with the Greek envoys.

The union was sealed on 6 July, when the Greek confession of faith was read and accepted in the pope's presence. Nine days later, on 15 July, Bonaventure died suddenly; the chronicle of his secretary alleged poison, but the cause cannot now be known. He was buried the next evening in the Franciscan church at Lyons, with the pope, the King of Aragon, and the council fathers at his funeral.

The council closed on 17 July, and the reunion it acclaimed was cast off at Constantinople within the decade. Bonaventure's relics fared ill — the Huguenots burned his body in the public square in 1562, and the head then rescued was lost in the French Revolution. Lyons had chosen him for a patron when his remains were found incorrupt in 1434.

events.title: The East-West Schism
events.shortBlurb: Papal legates laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, hardening the breach of East and West…
body: The estrangement of Latin West and Greek East, fed by language, rite, and the ambition of the see of Constantinople, broke into open quarrel in 1053, when the patriarch Michael Cerularius closed the Latin churches of the capital and struck the pope's name from the diptychs. Pope Leo IX sent legates under Cardinal Humbert of Moyenmoutier to treat with him.

The mission foundered on mutual distrust, and Leo died in April 1054 while the legates were still in the city. On 16 July 1054 they laid a bull of excommunication against Cerularius upon the altar of Hagia Sophia and departed; the patriarch answered with a synod that excommunicated the legates in turn.

The exchange concerned at first only persons, not whole Churches, but the other Eastern patriarchs gradually followed Constantinople, and the reunions sealed at Lyons in 1274 and Florence in 1439 did not hold. Convention dates the schism from that July day; the mutual censures of 1054 were lifted only on 7 December 1965, by Paul VI and the patriarch Athenagoras.

events.title: The Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
events.shortBlurb: The united Christian kings of Spain broke the power of the Almohads in the Reconquista's great turning point…
body: In 1195 the Almohads shattered Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos, and in 1211 the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir crossed from Morocco and took the Calatravan stronghold of Salvatierra. Alfonso appealed for a great counterstroke, and Innocent III preached the campaign as a crusade; besides the Castilians there gathered Peter II of Aragon, Sancho VII of Navarre, the military orders, and volunteers from Portugal and beyond the Pyrenees.

Guided through the Despenaperros pass by a local shepherd, the Christian host surprised the Almohad camp on 16 July 1212 at Las Navas de Tolosa in the Sierra Morena. In the close fighting the Castilian knights and the orders broke the enemy line, and Sancho of Navarre charged through to the caliph's own tent; al-Nasir fled, leaving his tent and standard to be sent to the pope.

The victory broke Almohad power in Spain. Baeza and Ubeda fell soon after, and within a generation Ferdinand III had taken Cordoba in 1236, Jaen in 1246, and Seville in 1248, while James I of Aragon won Valencia in 1238. Muslim Spain was reduced to the emirate of Granada, and the battle stands as the turning point of the Reconquista.

events.title: The Scillitan Martyrs
events.shortBlurb: Twelve African Christians were beheaded at Carthage in the earliest dated record of the Latin Church…
body: In the reign of Marcus Aurelius, twelve Christians of Scillium in Numidia, seven men and five women, were brought before the proconsul Vigellius Saturninus at Carthage. Their brief trial record, the Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs, is the earliest dated document of the Latin Church and the first to know a Latin Bible.

Offered thirty days in which to reconsider, their spokesman Speratus answered that in so good a cause there was no need of deliberation; and when pressed to swear by the genius of the emperor, he declared, "I recognize not the empire of this world; but rather do I serve that God whom no man hath seen." Saturninus pronounced sentence, and on 17 July 180 the twelve were beheaded.

Their names, Speratus, Nartzalus, Cittinus, Veturius, Felix, Aquilinus, Laetantius, Januaria, Generosa, Vestia, Donata, and Secunda, were kept in honor at Carthage, where a basilica rose over their memory. Tertullian, writing within a generation, numbers Saturninus among the first persecutors of the African church.

events.title: The Carmelites of Compiègne go to the guillotine
events.shortBlurb: Sixteen Carmelite nuns were executed in Paris, singing as they mounted the scaffold…
body: Their deaths came in the Terror's bloodiest weeks. Since the law of 22 Prairial — 10 June 1794 — the revolutionary tribunal of Paris, driven by the prosecutor Fouquier-Tinville, had condemned the accused without witnesses or defense, and the scaffold at the Place du Trône Renversé claimed more than thirteen hundred victims in six weeks.

The Carmelites were convicted on 17 July for living as a religious community and for the royalist letters found in their lodgings; with them died their friend Mulot de la Ménardière. Their bodies went with the day's other dead into the mass graves at Picpus, where their names are now inscribed among the 1,306 buried in the sand-pits there.

French Catholics soon linked their offering to the Terror's sudden end, for Robespierre fell ten days later. The memory of their death outlived the martyrology: it inspired Gertrud von Le Fort's novella The Song at the Scaffold in 1931, a drama by Georges Bernanos, and Francis Poulenc's opera Dialogues of the Carmelites, first staged at La Scala in 1957.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of the Martyrs of Compiègne (vatican.va)

events.title: The First Vatican Council defines papal infallibility
events.shortBlurb: The council solemnly defined the infallibility of the pope in the constitution Pastor Aeternus…
body: The First Vatican Council, convoked by Pius IX and opened in St Peter's on 8 December 1869 with some seven hundred fathers, first issued the constitution Dei Filius on faith and reason on 24 April 1870, then turned to the long-debated schema on the Roman Pontiff. A preliminary vote on 13 July showed 451 for the definition, 62 conditionally for it, and 88 against.

On 18 July 1870, as a thunderstorm broke over St Peter's, the fourth public session approved the constitution Pastor Aeternus by 433 votes to 2, the lone dissentients Bishops Riccio of Cajazzo and Fitzgerald of Little Rock. The constitution defined the pope's primacy of jurisdiction and, under carefully drawn conditions, his infallibility when he defines ex cathedra a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church.

Most of the minority had already left Rome, judging the definition inopportune rather than untrue, and all afterward accepted it. The next day France declared war on Prussia; in September Italian troops took Rome at the Porta Pia, and on 20 October 1870 Pius IX suspended the council, its work unfinished, leaving its remaining decrees to a future generation.

events.title: The suppression of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: Pope Clement XIV suppressed the Jesuits under pressure from the Catholic courts of Europe…
body: By the middle of the eighteenth century the Bourbon courts of Catholic Europe had turned against the Society of Jesus. Portugal drove the order out in 1759, France followed in 1764, and Spain and Naples in 1767; their ambassadors then besieged Rome itself, demanding the extinction of the whole Society and threatening a break with Rome if Clement XIV refused.

On 21 July 1773 the pope signed the brief Dominus ac Redemptor, suppressing the Society, then about twenty-three thousand strong, throughout the Church; it was published on 16 August, and the Jesuit general Lorenzo Ricci was arrested and died a prisoner in 1775, the charges against him never proven.

The brief could not be published everywhere. In Prussia and Russia the Protestant Frederick II and the Orthodox Catherine II, prizing the Jesuit schools, forbade its promulgation, and some two hundred fathers in White Russia kept the Society alive. On 7 August 1814, forty-one years after the suppression, Pope Pius VII by the bull Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum restored the Society to the universal Church.

events.title: The death of St. Bridget of Sweden
events.shortBlurb: The Swedish mystic and foundress died at Rome after years of labor for the Church…
body: Bridget's last years were spent at Rome, burdened by debts and by the enmity her plain speaking against abuses had earned. In 1372, though near seventy, she made a final pilgrimage to the Holy Land; at Bethlehem she received the vision of the Nativity — the Child lying radiant on the ground before the kneeling Virgin — that would reshape the image of Christ's birth in Western art.

She died at Rome on 23 July 1373 and was buried first at San Lorenzo in Panisperna. The next year her daughter Catherine bore her body home to Sweden, to Vadstena, the mother house of her order, where her relics are venerated to this day by Catholics and Lutherans together.

Her cause was pressed by Queen Margaret of Scandinavia, and Boniface IX canonized her on 7 October 1391; the Council of Constance confirmed the act in 1415. The return of the papacy from Avignon, for which she had pleaded so long, came four years after her death, when Gregory XI re-entered Rome in 1377, moved also by the pleading of Catherine of Siena.

events.title: The death of Thomas à Kempis
events.shortBlurb: The canon of the Devotio Moderna died at Mount St. Agnes, long held to be author of the Imitation of Christ…
body: Thomas Haemerken, Thomas of Kempen, was born about 1380 in that small Rhineland town, the son of a craftsman. Sent at thirteen to school at Deventer, he was formed by the Brethren of the Common Life, the followers of Geert Groote whose 'new devotion', the Devotio Moderna, taught a practical piety of humility, interior prayer, and the patient copying of good books.

In 1399 he entered the Augustinian canons of Mount St. Agnes near Zwolle, where his elder brother John was prior; he received the habit in 1406 and was ordained priest in 1413. For seventy-two years he served that house as novice master and twice as subprior, copying manuscripts, for he copied out the whole Bible four times, and writing small treatises of the spiritual life.

He died at Mount St. Agnes on 25 July 1471. By long tradition he is held to be the author of The Imitation of Christ, written in the years about 1418 to 1427; after the Sacred Scriptures no Christian book has been more translated or more read, and its quiet counsels of humility and detachment from the world have formed souls for five hundred years.

events.title: The fall of Robespierre and the end of the Terror
events.shortBlurb: The execution of Robespierre brought the Reign of Terror to a close and eased the persecution of the Church…
body: Maximilien Robespierre, born at Arras in 1758, rose through the Jacobin Club to dominate the Committee of Public Safety in the year of the Terror. On 8 June 1794 he presided over the Festival of the Supreme Being, the deist cult he had raised in place of the Church; two days later the Law of 22 Prairial stripped the Revolutionary Tribunal of every defense.

In the seven weeks that followed, the Paris guillotine claimed more than thirteen hundred lives. The Church suffered bitterly in those years, her refractory priests deported or drowned, and on 17 July 1794 sixteen Carmelite nuns of Compiègne mounted the scaffold singing, martyrs beatified in 1906.

On 27 July, 9 Thermidor, the Convention turned on him, voted his arrest, and outlawed him; cornered that night in the Hôtel de Ville, his jaw shattered by a pistol shot, he was guillotined the next evening, 28 July, with twenty-one of his partisans, among them Saint-Just and Couthon. His death broke the machinery of the Terror, and the persecution of the Church slowly eased.

events.title: St. Olaf falls at Stiklestad
events.shortBlurb: The king who worked to Christianize Norway was killed in battle and became the nation's patron…
body: Born about 995, Olaf Haraldsson spent his youth on Viking expeditions to the Baltic and England and was baptized at Rouen in Normandy. Returning in 1015, he made himself king of Norway and for thirteen years pressed the Christian faith on a half-pagan land, building churches and imposing the new law with a harshness that made enemies of the great chieftains.

In 1028, when Cnut the Great of Denmark and England claimed the Norwegian crown, the nobles abandoned Olaf, and he fled to the court of Yaroslav the Wise at Novgorod. Hearing that Cnut's regent, Jarl Håkon, had been lost at sea, he returned in 1030 with a small army, among them his young half-brother Harald Hardrada, to win back his kingdom.

On 29 July 1030, at Stiklestad, his host broke before the army of the chieftains and bonders, and the king was killed. Buried at Nidaros, he was declared a martyr on 3 August 1031 by Bishop Grimketel, miracles being reported at his grave. Dead, he did more for Norway's conversion than living: venerated as Rex Perpetuus Norvegiae, the eternal king of Norway, he became the nation's patron.

events.title: The First Defenestration of Prague
events.shortBlurb: Hussite crowds threw the town councillors from the windows of the New Town Hall, igniting the Hussite Wars…
body: Jan Hus, burned at Constance on 6 July 1415 despite a safe-conduct from King Sigismund, left Bohemia seething with anger. Among his followers in Prague the radical priest Jan Želivský drew great crowds to the church of Our Lady of the Snows, and when the council of the New Town refused to release imprisoned Hussites, the city stood at the edge of revolt.

On 30 July 1419, after Želivský's sermon, the procession marched on the New Town Hall; in the tumult the crowd stormed the building and hurled the burgomaster and a dozen councillors and officials from the windows, and those not killed by the fall were finished by the mob below. In the crowd that day, making his first mark, was the squire Jan Žižka.

King Wenceslaus IV died of apoplexy on 16 August, seventeen days later. His brother Sigismund was rejected by the Hussites, and Pope Martin V preached a crusade against them, five in all between 1420 and 1431, all broken by the wagon-fort armies of Žižka and, after his death in 1424, of Prokop the Great. The conflict lasted until the defeat of the radicals at Lipany in 1434.

events.title: The death of St. Ignatius of Loyola
events.shortBlurb: The founder of the Society of Jesus died at Rome as his young order spread across the world…
body: In his last years Ignatius lived quietly at Rome, governing by letter a Society that in sixteen years had grown from ten companions to about a thousand members on both sides of the Atlantic. At the urging of his sons he dictated the story of his conversion to Father Luis Goncalves da Camara, the plain account since known as his Autobiography.

In the summer of 1556 he was seized by Roman fever. On 30 July he sent his secretary Polanco to beg a last blessing of Pope Paul IV, but the physicians saw no danger and the errand was put off till morning. At dawn on 31 July he was found peacefully dying, and he passed before the holy oils could be brought.

He was buried at Santa Maria della Strada, where now the Gesu stands and his tomb is venerated. Diego Lainez was chosen to succeed him as general. Beatified by Paul V in 1609, Ignatius was canonized by Gregory XV in 1622, in the same ceremony as Francis Xavier and Teresa of Avila.

events.title: The Pardon of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: The great indulgence tradition holds St. Francis obtained for pilgrims to the little chapel of the Portiuncula…
body: The Portiuncula, the 'little portion', was a ruined chapel of St. Mary of the Angels below Assisi, given to Francis and his first brothers by the Benedictines of Monte Subasio. Francis rebuilt it with his own hands and made it the home of his young order; here in 1212 he received Clare and cut her hair, and here he died on 3 October 1226.

Here, by a tradition the Franciscan sources fix in 1216, the Pardon of Assisi began. Praying one night, Francis saw Christ and his Mother amid a host of angels and asked that all who entered the little church, repentant and confessed, might receive full pardon of their sins. He hastened to Pope Honorius III, then at Perugia, who granted the unheard-of gift of a plenary indulgence.

The indulgence could be gained in the chapel from first vespers of 1 August to sunset of 2 August, as is still kept; later popes extended the Pardon, under the usual conditions of confession, Communion, and prayer for the pope's intentions, to parish churches everywhere. The little chapel itself stands enshrined today within the basilica of St. Mary of the Angels, raised from 1569 to shelter it.

events.title: The martyrdom of Pope St. Sixtus II
events.shortBlurb: A pope was cut down with his deacons at the altar in the Roman catacombs under the persecution of Valerian…
body: Early in August 258 the Emperor Valerian sharpened his persecution with a second edict: bishops, priests, and deacons were to be put to death at once, and Christians forbidden to gather in the cemeteries. The blow fell first on Rome, where Sixtus II had sat as pope for a year, having succeeded Stephen I in August 257.

On 6 August, as Sixtus sat teaching the brethren in a catacomb on the Appian Way, soldiers seized him and beheaded him. Four of his seven deacons died with him, as Cyprian of Carthage wrote in a letter; two more, Felicissimus and Agapitus, were cut down the same day in the cemetery of Praetextatus. The pope's body was laid in the papal crypt of the cemetery of Callixtus.

Four days later, on 10 August, his archdeacon Lawrence followed him to death; that same autumn Cyprian himself was martyred at Carthage. Rome kept the memory green: Sixtus was named in the canon of the Roman Mass among the first martyrs after the apostles, Pope Damasus adorned his tomb with verses, and his feast on 6 August appears already in the fourth-century calendar.

events.title: The death of Pope St. Paul VI
events.shortBlurb: The pope who brought the Second Vatican Council to its close died on the feast of the Transfiguration…
body: Giovanni Battista Montini was born on 26 September 1897 at Concesio, near Brescia. Ordained in 1920, he served more than thirty years in the Secretariat of State under Pius XI and Pius XII, then governed Milan as archbishop from 1954, until his election as pope on 21 June 1963, taking the name Paul VI.

He reconvened the Second Vatican Council after John XXIII's death and closed it on 8 December 1965, then bore the weight of its reception: the revised Roman Missal and the reform of the curia. He was the first pope to travel by air, journeying to the Holy Land in 1964, to the United Nations in 1965 to plead 'no more war', and in all to six continents.

His encyclicals included Populorum progressio on the development of peoples (1967) and Humanae vitae on the transmission of life (1968), the latter answered by dissent. Worn by grief at the murder of his friend Aldo Moro that May, he died of a heart attack at Castel Gandolfo on the evening of 6 August 1978, the feast of the Transfiguration; he was canonized by Pope Francis on 14 October 2018.

sources.text: Vatican biography, Canonization of St. Paul VI (vatican.va)

events.title: The Battle of Lechfeld
events.shortBlurb: The defeat of the raiding Magyars by Otto the Great turned Hungary toward settlement and the Christian faith…
body: For half a century the mounted archers of the Magyars had ridden out of the Danube basin to plunder Christendom, striking Italy, France, and the Low Countries. In the summer of 955 a great host under the chieftain Bulcsú swept into Bavaria and on 8 August laid siege to Augsburg, whose walls its bishop, Ulrich, rallied the townsfolk to defend.

King Otto I, gathering contingents from every duchy and a thousand Bohemians, met the invaders on 10 August, the feast of St. Lawrence, on the Lechfeld, the plain of the river Lech. The Magyar feigned retreat failed; their host was driven into the river and destroyed in the pursuit. Conrad the Red, the king's reconciled son-in-law, fell in the victory, and Bulcsú and the chieftain Lehel were hanged at Regensburg.

The soldiers hailed Otto on the field as father of the fatherland; in 962 he was crowned emperor at Rome. The raids of the Magyars were ended for good. Settled now in the Danube plain, the Hungarian people turned within two generations to the faith of those they had raided: Duke Géza was baptized, and his son Stephen was crowned in the year 1000 as first king of Christian Hungary.

events.title: The founding of the Society of Jesus
events.shortBlurb: On the feast of the Assumption, Ignatius of Loyola and his companions bound themselves by vow at Montmartre…
body: Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque courtier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona in 1521, had been converted during his convalescence and schooled in prayer at Manresa. Studying at the University of Paris from 1528, he won six companions: Peter Faber of Savoy, Francis Xavier of Navarre, Diego Laínez, Alfonso Salmerón, Nicolás Bobadilla, and the Portuguese Simão Rodrigues.

On 15 August 1534, the feast of the Assumption, the seven climbed Montmartre and in a chapel bound themselves by vows of poverty and chastity and a promise to sail for Jerusalem to labor for souls; should that prove impossible, they would place themselves at the disposal of the pope. Faber, the only priest among them, offered the Mass at which the vow was made.

In 1537 they reunited at Venice, and when war with the Turks blocked their sailing, they were ordained priests and went to Rome. Pope Paul III approved their Company of Jesus in the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae of 27 September 1540, and the companions elected Ignatius their first general. Within a generation the Society had become a force of education, mission, and reform.

events.title: The sack of Rome by Alaric
events.shortBlurb: The Visigoths breached the walls of the eternal city, shaking the ancient world and moving Augustine to write…
body: Alaric, king of the Visigoths, had besieged Rome twice since 408, once setting up a puppet emperor. When his talks with the Emperor Honorius at Ravenna broke down, he marched on the city a third time, and in the night of 24 August 410 his Goths entered by the Salarian Gate. Rome had not fallen to an enemy in eight hundred years.

For three days the Goths plundered. Alaric, an Arian Christian, forbade his men to violate the basilicas, and the churches of St. Peter and St. Paul filled with fugitives whom no Gothic hand touched. Yet palaces were burned and captives led away, among them Galla Placidia, the emperor's half-sister. Alaric died before the year's end in Calabria and was buried in the bed of the river Busento.

The shock ran through the world. From Bethlehem Jerome wrote that the brightest light of the world had gone out, that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken; pagans answered that Rome fell because the old gods were forsaken. To refute them Augustine of Hippo began in 413 his City of God, setting the passing city of man against the city that endures.

events.title: The St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre
events.shortBlurb: A wave of killing of French Protestants that began in Paris on the feast of St. Bartholomew stands as one of the tragedies of the Wars of Religion…
body: In August 1572 the Protestant nobility of France crowded into Paris for the wedding of Henry of Navarre to Margaret of Valois, sister of King Charles IX, a match meant to seal the Peace of Saint-Germain and pause ten years of religious war. On 22 August a shot fired from a window wounded the Huguenot leader, Admiral Gaspard de Coligny.

In the night of 23 to 24 August, by decision of the king's council, men of the Duke of Guise murdered Coligny in his lodging and threw his body from the window. The killing spread: for three days Paris hunted Protestants in its streets and houses, and two or three thousand died in the city; Navarre and his cousin Condé escaped the sword by a forced conversion.

Over the following weeks the massacre was imitated in Orléans, Lyon, Rouen, and Bordeaux, the dead of that summer reckoned from five to thirty thousand. At Rome the news was read as a deliverance: Gregory XIII ordered a Te Deum and struck a medal. The Wars of Religion burned on until Henry of Navarre, crowned Henry IV, gave France the Edict of Nantes in 1598.

events.title: The death of St. Louis IX on crusade
events.shortBlurb: The holy king of France died of disease in the crusader camp before the walls of Tunis…
body: In 1267 Louis took the cross a second time, and the expedition was steered toward North Africa: the emir of Tunis, Muhammad al-Mustansir, was reported ready to consider baptism, and the king's brother Charles of Anjou, newly master of Sicily, had designs of his own. Landing near Carthage in July 1270, the crusaders waited for Charles's fleet.

In the August heat dysentery swept the camp; the king's son John Tristan died in early August, and soon the king himself lay sick. He had himself laid on a bed of ashes strewn in the form of a cross, and died on 25 August, his last cries, says his confessor Geoffrey of Beaulieu, of Jerusalem. Charles's ships reached the camp that very day.

Two days later his son was proclaimed king as Philip III. The crusade dissolved: Charles made a profitable treaty with the emir in October and withdrew, while Edward of England, arriving too late, sailed on to Acre. Louis's heart was borne to Monreale and his bones to Saint-Denis; within a generation he was canonized.

events.title: The Battle of Manzikert
events.shortBlurb: The Byzantine defeat that opened Asia Minor to the Turks and set the stage for the Crusades…
body: On 26 August 1071, near the town of Manzikert in Armenia, north of Lake Van, the army of the Byzantine emperor Romanus IV Diogenes met the Seljuk Turks under Sultan Alp Arslan, the 'Heroic Lion.' When the Turkish horse-archers wore down the imperial host and the reserve under Andronicus Doukas abandoned the field, the emperor's division was surrounded, and Romanus, wounded, was taken prisoner.

Alp Arslan treated his captive with honour and released him within days for a ransom, tribute, and a marriage alliance; but Constantinople had already acclaimed his stepson Michael VII, and Romanus, seized by his enemies, was blinded so savagely that he died of the ordeal in 1072. Alp Arslan himself outlived the battle by barely a year, stabbed by a condemned prisoner in November 1072.

The battle cost fewer lives than legend says, but its consequences were immense: with no army left to hold the frontier, Turkish tribes spread across Asia Minor, the ancient heartland of Eastern Christianity, taking Nicaea itself within a few years. The emperors' desperate appeals for Western aid helped move Pope Urban II, a generation later, to preach the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095.

events.title: The death of Pope Sixtus V
events.shortBlurb: The vigorous reforming pope who rebuilt Rome and reorganized the Curia died after a brief but momentous reign…
body: Felice Peretti, born of poor parents at Grottammare near Montalto on 13 December 1521, entered the Franciscans as a boy and won fame as a preacher, counting among his friends Philip Neri and Ignatius of Loyola. Made cardinal by Pius V in 1570, he lived in studious obscurity under Gregory XIII until his election as pope on 24 April 1585, when he took the name Sixtus V.

His five years refounded papal government. The bull Immensa Aeterni Dei of 1588 organized the Curia into fifteen permanent congregations, and he fixed the number of cardinals at seventy. Stern justice stamped out the brigandage that had infested the Papal States, and an iron economy filled the treasury he had found empty.

He set Rome on new lines: Domenico Fontana raised the Vatican obelisk before St. Peter's in 1586, the dome of the basilica was completed, and the Acqua Felice brought water to the hills. His corrected Vulgate of 1590 was withdrawn after his death for its errors. Worn by toil and fever, he died at the Quirinal on 27 August 1590 and was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore.

events.title: The death of St. Augustine and the siege of Hippo
events.shortBlurb: The great bishop and Doctor died as the Vandals pressed their siege against his African city…
body: In 429 the Vandal king Genseric led his people from Spain into Roman Africa, and by the early summer of 430 his host stood before Hippo, where the defeated Count Boniface commanded the defense. Bishops driven from their sees crowded into the city, among them Possidius of Calama, Augustine's friend of forty years and his first biographer.

The siege held nearly fourteen months. In its third month Augustine fell mortally ill; he had the penitential psalms written out in large letters and hung on the walls about his bed, and for his last ten days would see no one but his physicians. He died on 28 August 430, in his seventy-sixth year, leaving no will, for he had nothing to leave but his books.

Hippo outlasted him by months before the Vandals took and burned it in 431; yet his library in the basilica escaped the flames, and his writings fed the West thereafter. His relics were later carried to Sardinia and thence to Pavia, and the Church of Roman Africa wasted under a century of Arian Vandal rule.

events.title: The Battle of Mohács
events.shortBlurb: The Ottoman victory that broke the kingdom of Hungary and opened Central Europe to Turkish advance…
body: On 29 August 1526, on the plain of Mohács beside the Danube, some twenty-six thousand Hungarians under the twenty-year-old King Louis II faced the far greater host of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. The Hungarian charge shattered on the Ottoman artillery and the volleys of the janissaries, and within two hours the royal army was annihilated; among the dead were twenty-eight barons and seven prelates.

The commander-in-chief, Pál Tomori, archbishop of Kalocsa, fell with his men, and with him László Szalkai, archbishop of Esztergom. The king, fleeing the field through the evening rain, was thrown from his horse and drowned in the flooded Csele stream. He left no heir, and the broken kingdom elected two rival kings: John Zápolya, voivode of Transylvania, and Ferdinand of Habsburg.

Suleiman entered Buda unopposed and burned it, carrying off its treasures; the Turks returned to hold it in 1541, and Hungary lay split for a century and a half between the Ottoman plain, the Habsburg borderland, and vassal Transylvania. The medieval kingdom that had stood as Christendom's eastern bulwark was gone, and three years after Mohács the sultan's army stood before Vienna itself.

events.title: The September Massacres of Paris
events.shortBlurb: Revolutionary mobs stormed the Paris prisons and slaughtered priests and religious who had refused the oath against the Church…
body: In the summer of 1792 the Revolution slid toward terror. The manifesto of the invading Duke of Brunswick threatened Paris with destruction, and on 10 August the crowd stormed the Tuileries and brought down the monarchy. The radical Commune filled the prisons with suspects, and on 2 September came word that Verdun, the last fortress on the road to Paris, had fallen to the Prussians.

That afternoon the slaughter began, fed by Marat's incitement and by the fear that the prisoners would break out once the volunteers had marched. For four days makeshift tribunals sat at the Abbaye, La Force, and the other prisons, and the condemned were hacked down at the gates, while the Commune tolerated, and in part paid, the killers.

By 6 September about half the prison population of Paris, some twelve to fourteen hundred persons, had perished, among them some two hundred and forty priests, though most were common criminals; with them died the queen's friend, the Princesse de Lamballe. The massacres, imitated in provincial towns, horrified Europe and opened the road to the Terror.

events.title: St. Gregory the Great is consecrated Pope
events.shortBlurb: The reluctant monk was consecrated Bishop of Rome and began a pontificate that would reshape the medieval Church…
body: The year 589 closed in disaster for Rome: the Tiber burst its banks, sweeping away houses and the granaries of the Church, and pestilence followed on the flood. In February 590 Pope Pelagius II died of the plague, and the clergy and people with one mind chose Gregory, abbot of St. Andrew's, to succeed him.

Gregory shrank from the office. He wrote to the Emperor Maurice begging him not to confirm the election, but the prefect Germanus suppressed the letter; and tradition adds that he fled the city in a merchant's basket and lay hidden until he was found. While awaiting the emperor's answer he ordered a sevenfold litany, seven companies processing from seven churches to St. Mary Major to beg the plague's end.

Legend holds that as the procession passed the mausoleum of Hadrian he saw the archangel Michael sheathe his sword above it, whence its name Castel Sant'Angelo. The imperial assent came at last, and on 3 September 590 the reluctant monk, the first to take the papal throne, was consecrated; on that day, since his death date falls in Lent, his feast is kept.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "Pope St. Gregory I (the Great)"

events.title: The fall of the Western Roman Empire
events.shortBlurb: The last emperor in the West was deposed, and the Church became the enduring institution of a collapsing world…
body: In August 476 the barbarian soldiers of Italy — Heruli, Rugii, and Sciri among them — rose under their commander Odoacer to claim the lands promised them, and put the general Orestes to death at Piacenza. On 4 September Odoacer entered Ravenna and compelled Orestes' young son, the emperor Romulus, mockingly styled Augustulus, 'little Augustus,' to lay down the purple.

Sparing the boy with a pension and a villa in Campania, Odoacer sent the imperial insignia to the Emperor Zeno at Constantinople and ruled Italy as king under the East's nominal overlordship. No emperor reigned again in the West: Julius Nepos, the last claimant recognized by Constantinople, held out in Dalmatia only until 480. Later ages fixed on this quiet abdication as the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

The change was less a single blow than the last step of a long dissolution. As civil authority failed, the Catholic Church remained the one institution spanning the old empire: her bishops kept order in the cities, her monasteries guarded learning, and the see of Rome became the fixed point of the West — the vision Augustine, dead a generation before at besieged Hippo, had framed in his City of God.

events.title: The lifting of the Great Siege of Malta
events.shortBlurb: The Knights of St. John broke the Ottoman siege of Malta, and Christendom credited the deliverance to Our Lady on the feast of her Nativity…
body: On 18 May 1565 an Ottoman armada of some two hundred galleys and forty thousand men, sent by Suleiman the Magnificent under Mustafa Pasha and the admiral Piyale, descended on Malta. Against them stood the seventy-year-old Grand Master of the Knights of St. John, Jean Parisot de la Valette, with some seven hundred knights and perhaps nine thousand soldiers and Maltese.

Fort St. Elmo, guarding the harbour mouth, endured a month of bombardment and assault, costing the Turks thousands of men and the famed corsair Dragut, before it fell on 23 June and nearly all its defenders. The struggle closed in on Birgu and Senglea, where La Valette, pike in hand, repelled the great August assaults. On 7 September the Sicilian relief gathered by Don García de Toledo landed at last.

The exhausted Ottomans re-embarked, their last ships sailing on 11 September. Because the deliverance was linked to the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin on 8 September, Malta kept that day as Il-Vitorja, Victory Day, crediting Our Lady with the rescue; and the next spring La Valette founded on Mount Sciberras the new fortress city that still bears his name.

events.title: The relief of Vienna
events.shortBlurb: A Christian army under John III Sobieski broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, and the pope extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary in thanksgiving…
body: On 14 July 1683 a vast Ottoman army under the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa closed around Vienna, defended by Count Rüdiger von Starhemberg with a garrison that dwindled under two months of mining and assault. The city's appeals went out across Christendom, and Pope Innocent XI laboured to knit the princes into an alliance, sending the Capuchin Marco d'Aviano as his legate to the gathering relief.

King John III Sobieski of Poland, who had placed his army under the protection of Our Lady of Częstochowa, took command of the Polish, imperial, and German forces. On the morning of 12 September Marco d'Aviano celebrated Mass on the Kahlenberg heights; then the allies swept down, and Sobieski's charge of some eighteen thousand horse, the largest cavalry charge of the age, broke the Ottoman army to flight.

Vienna was delivered, and the fleeing Kara Mustafa paid for the disaster with his life, strangled at Belgrade on Christmas Day by the sultan's order. In thanksgiving Innocent XI extended to the whole Church the feast of the Most Holy Name of Mary, kept on 12 September, the anniversary of the battle; and the Holy League he formed in 1684 carried the war on into Hungary.

sources.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1913), "The Holy Name of Mary"

events.title: The death of St. John Chrysostom in exile
events.shortBlurb: The great preacher and archbishop of Constantinople died on the road of a second banishment, blessing God to the end…
body: John, born at Antioch about 349 and ordained its priest in 386, preached there for twelve years with such power that men called him Chrysostom, the 'golden-mouthed.' Made archbishop of Constantinople in 398, he reformed a worldly clergy and rebuked the court without fear, earning the enmity of the Empress Eudoxia and of Theophilus of Alexandria, who had him deposed at the Synod of the Oak in 403.

Briefly recalled, he was banished again in 404 to Cucusus in Armenia, whence his letters still heartened the Church. In the summer of 407 he was ordered to Pityus, at the far end of the Black Sea; marched on foot through heat and storm, he sank at Comana in Pontus and died there on 14 September 407. His last recorded words were 'Glory to God for all things.'

In 438 the Emperor Theodosius II, son of the Eudoxia who had exiled him, brought his relics to Constantinople and laid them in the Church of the Holy Apostles, begging pardon for his mother. East and West venerate him as a Doctor of the Church; and because 14 September belongs to the Holy Cross, the West keeps his feast on the thirteenth.

events.title: The dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.shortBlurb: Constantine's great basilica over Calvary and the tomb of Christ was dedicated at Jerusalem, giving rise to the feast of the Holy Cross…
body: After his victory over Licinius Constantine wrote to Macarius, bishop of Jerusalem, ordering a basilica surpassing all others over the tomb of Christ; the temple of Venus that Hadrian had planted over the site was torn down, and the tomb laid bare. Over the holy places rose the great Martyrium basilica, the courtyard about Calvary, and the rotunda of the Anastasis, which Eusebius called a New Jerusalem.

In 335, at the close of the Council of Tyre, Constantine bade the assembled bishops pass on to Jerusalem for the consecration, which fell on 13 and 14 September, and Eusebius himself pronounced the orations. On the second day, tradition records, Bishop Macarius lifted up the wood of the Cross before the people; and the anniversary, the Encaenia, was kept for eight days, drawing monks from Mesopotamia, Syria, and Egypt.

The church stood until the Persian sack of 614, and, rebuilt by the monk Modestus, until the caliph al-Hakim razed it in 1009. The church of the Crusaders, consecrated in 1149 over Calvary and the tomb, is the one that pilgrims enter today, nearly seventeen centuries after the bishops of Tyre kept the first Encaenia.

events.title: The martyrdom of St. Cyprian of Carthage
events.shortBlurb: The bishop and great writer of the African Church was beheaded before his people in the persecution of Valerian…
body: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, born about 210 of a wealthy pagan family of Carthage and won to Christ in middle life, was chosen bishop of that city about 249. He guided the African Church through the Decian persecution, the bitter controversy over the readmission of the lapsed, and a wasting plague, and disputed with Pope Stephen I over baptism conferred by heretics.

When the Emperor Valerian renewed the persecution, Cyprian was examined on 30 August 257 by the proconsul Aspasius Paternus and banished to Curubis. Recalled the next year under a sterner edict, he waited quietly in his gardens until the guard came; on 14 September 258 the proconsul Galerius Maximus read the sentence, that Thascius Cyprian should die by the sword. Cyprian answered, 'Deo gratias' — Thanks be to God.

Before a vast crowd of his people he knelt and was beheaded outside the city, having bidden his friends give the executioner twenty-five gold pieces. His deacon Pontius wrote his Life, and the court record of his trial, the Acta proconsularia, survives entire. The first African bishop to win the martyr's crown, he is kept on 16 September together with Pope Cornelius, his ally and fellow martyr.

events.title: The stigmata of St. Francis of Assisi
events.shortBlurb: On the mountain of La Verna, St. Francis received in his own body the wounds of the crucified Christ…
body: In August 1224 Francis of Assisi, already worn by austerity and failing sight, withdrew with a few companions to Mount La Verna in the Tuscan Apennines, a lonely crag given him years before by Count Orlando of Chiusi. There he kept the 'Lent of St. Michael,' forty days of fasting and prayer from the Assumption to Michaelmas, absorbed in meditation on the Passion of Christ.

About the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, as Brother Leo and the earliest Lives relate, there appeared to him a seraph, six-winged, bearing the figure of a man nailed to a cross. When the vision passed, Francis found in his own hands, feet, and side the marks of the Crucified: nail-heads of blackened flesh, and a wound in his side that often bled.

Francis bore the wounds for the two years that remained to him, hiding them beneath his habit until his death on 3 October 1226; Thomas of Celano soon recorded them, and Bonaventure set them at the heart of his great Life.
